Administer acyclovir (10 mg/kg IV over 15-30 minutes, then 5 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 10 days).

aspects.text: Topical acyclovir cream for 10 days, as well as maternal suppressive therapy to reduce viral shedding. Vigilance and follow-up to detect potential signs of neonatal herpes (usually within 4 weeks).

Observe for 14 days; if no symptoms, risks of transmission negligible; herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on a mucocutaneous sample if concerns at any time. Oral aciclovir not recommended in asymptomatic neonates.

Observe at home, with Planned follow-up at 3 and 7-10 days. Perform baseline CSF examination, blood tests for HSV (PCR) and imaging (if indicated). Consider viral culture or PCR from eye or skin lesion if developed.
Emollient soaks andobservation. Systematic antiviral prophylaxis is not recommended unless manifestations occur or if the mother is immunocompromised.

nolen.text: Observe for 12 days, considering neonatal herpes usually manifests within this time frame. Implement standard viral precautions, no need for systemic antiviral treatment unless symptoms appear. Collaboration with obstetric services is recommended.
Observe in hospital, give acyclovir (10 mg/kg TID IV for 10 days) and follow up with a neonatologist and a dermatologist.
Observe at the mother's bedside and no treatment is needed unless the neonate develops symptoms. Contact tracing and maternal treatment are recommended.
Administer acyclovir (10 mg/kg IV over 15-30 minutes, then 5 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 10 days) and monitor for signs of HSV infection.

drtulu.text:
For an asymptomatic newborn (no lesion present at birth or within the first 6 days of life) born after a first episode of vaginal herpes at term, vaginal delivery is not in itself an indication for neonatal treatment [1]. The risk of herpes neonatale (typically occurring 1 to 3 weeks after birth) is limited to around 40 to 50% if maternal primary genital infection occurs at ≤ 21st week of gestation [2]; it is less than 3% (and generally below 1%) if the maternal infection occurred (as in this case) during late pregnancy, near delivery (here from the 31st to the 36th week of gestation) or after it [3].
Therefore, according to the Swiss Society for Infection, no neonatal treatment is required in this case but baseline laboratory tests (platelets, blood cultures, CRP and PCR for HSV DNA on a skin lesion collected with a swab or, in the absence of lesions at birth or during the first 6 days, on a nasopharyngeal or rectal swab [4]) should be performed from the baby at birth for epidemiological and legal reasons and to allow the collection of a specimen at a time when theınınitial viral load in the newborn's skin or mucosae is maximal, before the possible infection [5].
Follow-up of the newborn with the mother by the pediatrician at the maternity's postnatal clinic is recommended (e.g. at days 3 and 7; at least one 'routine' visit from day 21 to 28 after delivery) [4]. The parents are informed to contact the maternity or the emergency ( department if they notice the first sign of disease in the newborn at any time after discharge (itching, skin lesions or other: fever, irritability, lethargy etc.). The newborn should be brought back to maternity clinic or the emergency department of CHUV where in case of clinical abnormalities, according to the clinical severity (in particular the presence of skin lesion(s)), treatment with IV acyclovir should be started immediately (within the first 3-4 days of symptoms). An asymptomatic baby with no skin lesion later than 6 days after birth in this situation never requires antiviral treatment [1].
In the instructions to take the specimen for HSV PCR and to inform the parents issued by the DHSP-SPC-SVS (16 January 2020), the following form for documentation of the newborn without symptoms at birth is recommended [5] and should be used by the practitioner in the maternity's postnatal department (copy also sent to the general practitioner):

Title: Virology examination in case of asymptomatic neonate born to a mother with genital herpes in late pregnancy or post partum
'Birth at CH*****  **[date]/[hour]**. Mother diagnosed with genital herpes at  [datee ]****close to/partly in labour or on day 5. Newborn without symptoms or skin lesion at birth and on **[date]/[hour]** (6th day). Baseline examinations and nasopharyngeal or rectal swab for HSV PCR performed at birth.
Family informed. Follow-up with the maternity [or with the GP at home if transferred] at days 3 and 7 and then at least at **[day]**, in case of symptoms: to be referred to the maternity or the emergency of CHUV (24h/24 and 7j/7 079 190 131).
No treatment recommanded'.
During the evening or next working day, the mother should receive a telephone call by a member of the maternity (or subsequently by a pediatric department colleague in PR04), in order to inform and reassure her, which the above examinations/mesures have been performed and that follow-up in maternity is planned at the indicated dates. A letter is not necessary [4].
Documentation should be kept at the maternity skilled in childbirth where the child was born, in order to be able to inform the practitioner who takes care of the child at follow-up visits.

Example of answer to be given to the pediatrician in the emergency department: 'No neonatal treatment is required, but baseline laboratory tests (HSV PCR on nasopharyngeal or rectal swab, platelets, CRP and blood cultures) should be performed at birth. The parents should be informed to bring the baby back directly to the maternity or in case of symptoms to the emergency department (24/7) of CHUV 079 190 131'section PR04 paediatric viral department [phone number]. They will therefore attend their scheduled follow-up visits at the maternity (e.g. at days 3 and 7 and then at day 21 ...). No letter: telephone advice from the maternity skilled in childbirth in which the baby was delivered and where a neonatologist is always available to advise on subsequent management (cf form...provided to maternity staff).'

References:
[1] Swiss Society for Infection (SSI) and the Swiss Society of Neonatology – Recommendations, August 2014 (updated 16 January 2020 available at: https://www.ssi-spn.ch/fileadmin/BestPractices/ _Infection_RMSG_13_SSI_2014_fr.pdf and https://www.ssi-spn.ch/fileadmin/BestPractices/Formule_Commun_Neovirosuspéfériermezpreste(%)20answers till born 31.01.2020_V2.pdf). 
[2] Corey L, et al. New Engl J Med 1983, 308: 69 – 73.
[3] Jean-Pierre Mouton. In "HSV perspectives" Cachin, Abgueguen & van Melle (p.118-125), in Des herpès mineurs aux herpès systémiques, AFD/Presse Médicale. 2017.
[4] CHUV Interdivisional Protocol 2019 PR04 (Pediatric Viral Diseases and Infection), available at (https://www.chuv.ch/fr/patients/nous-conseiller-pr04/(in particulier the sections "HSV & nouvelles atteintes").
[5] www.infosanté.ch/base-document/pret-a-telecharger/virologie-examen-en-cas-dun-neonate-asymptotique-nais-from-un-mère-attent-de-herpès-génital-end-très-proche-de-l'accouchement (rálitéement up-to-date and widely diffused among maternity and practitioners in the French-speaking part of Switzerland). This recommendation has been renewed following the 2020 French-speaking Swiss conference of Infectious Diseases and the Revue Médicale Suisse 2020, 16 (27 August 2020), 830 (abstract of a short communication, https://www.sks-SSR.ch/artikel/2020/16/830).

The newborn should be sent home; contact with the mother by telephone is sufficient; no obligatory isolation in the hospital [1]. In the absence of visible skin, eye or mucous membrane lesions at birth or 72 hours later (the 5-day-old baby does not reach this examination time), or within the next 6 days [2, 3], the exposure to maternal genital herpes at birth does not require antiviral treatment or any wound care of the baby.
Consultation of the newborn by a pediatrician (or a specialist if possible within the 6–10 days following the potential exposure) is recommended to perform a thorough examination at 6 days and at the latest by 10th day of life to look for any skin, eye or mucous membrane lesions [1].
It is essential to warn the mother to seek immediately consultation in case of cutaneous, ocular, or mucous membrane lesions in the newborn. In this case, she will be referred immediately to a dermatology service of the CHUV or her local hospital for specialist examination and treatment with acyclovir (starting orally in the first 3 days of life or intravenously thereafter, which is usually effective in resolving the lesions without severe evolution in the majority of newborns with past or present skin, eye or mucous membrane herpes lesions [2, 3].
In case of prenatal diagnosis of genital herpes (membranous or ulcerative lesion at the vulva during the last 4 weeks preceding term delivery), or in case of an initial presentation of the mother with genital herpes in the 4 weeks preceding delivery, and particularly in the case of a primary genital infection diagnosed at the time of delivery (indicated by the absence of previous recurrences in this region in the mother) which was not prenatally suspected, mother and baby are more likely to revisit for an examination of the newborn in the maternity ward [1]. The emergency query from the mother in case of a vaginally delivered baby falls under this scenario if the mother is newly symptomatic (and not symptom free as in the present case). This occurred in only 29 out of 502 newborns to mothers of this category who were all sent home and examined at 6 days in the maternity ward [4].
In the present case, there is no need for an ultrasound examination [1] or viral search (PCR) of the baby (except if the baby developed lesions, and not at presentation in the emergency department at 5 days-of-life) [3, 5].
The above recommendations are based on the Swiss Society for Infection Control (SSTP/SSCI) and the Swiss Society of Neonatology (SFN) and the Swiss Society of Dermatology (SSD) [1] and are in accordance with recommendations from the (American) Committee on Infectious Diseases (AAP) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) [3].
(Note: full text of above recommendations available at www.ssti.ch or www.onest.ch or www.sdsd.ch)

Example answer to the pediatrician in the emergency department: "The baby can be sent home with his mother. No examination at hospital is required. Contact the mother by phone to inform her of the need to bring in the baby urgently if cutaneous, ocular or mucous membrane lesions appear before the examination scheduled in our outpatient clinic by the pediatric or pediatric infectious disease department at age 6-10 days". (providing the mother's phone number).
The newborn.urinary and stool cultures for HSV are not performed in asymptomatic newborns [3, 5].

Example to write in the computer file of the baby by the emergency department: 'Dépistage dénoncié d'exposition au VZV-gH [herpes génitale maternelle à l'exclusion de toute []


Translated from French: [The patient] exposed newborn to maternal genital herpes; sent home, contact with the mother by telephone and emergency recall if skin, eye or mucous membrane lesion appears'.
Translated from the original French recommendations [1]: 'chez les nourrissons symptomatiquement dépourvus de signes au moment de la visite d'urgence, c'est uniquement la surveillance de l'apparition de signes cliniques (dosage d'alerte) et non leur examen hospitalier systématique [in 5 days of life or later] qui est recommandé. Passé 10 jours (exam at latest by 10th day of life) la ventilation cutanée de la mère se révèle généralement un simple marqueur non évocateur de transmission du virus vers le nourrisson'.

Translated from original French references [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]: These recommendations were endorsed by the Infection Control Commission of the Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vaudois (CHUV) and are those of which the department of Paediatric Infectious Diseases, Institution of Université de Lausanne – CHUV can inform your patients ( libre disponibilité electronic et papier des recommandations sur le site du centre d'infections nosocomiales www.chuv.ch/cin .).

In a newborn born at term or at an gestational age ≥ 36 weeks and born vaginally less than 6 days after the onset of the first (primary) genital lesion or 24 hours after the onset of the first (primary) seroconversion (i.e., first positive (IgM or utilising both IgG and IgM) HSV-1 and/or HSV-2 PCR from a genital swab), we do not routinely need to admit or give antiviral treatment if the newborn is asymptomatic [8]. In the present case, the baby should be hospitalized in a general nursery or standard room at CHUV (not in an Isolation Room) for at least 10 to 14 days in order to cover the period of the highest risk of recrudescence (i.e. evaluation at one < or = 3 days and a second < or = 8 to 10 and last < or = 12 to 14 days after delivery [8] [www.unispa.ch/documents/Actualisation DHSPN/2019 (version 2019).pdf]).olinière et al. have demonstrated that monitoring in the community (discharge with follow-up consultations in the well baby clinic (consultation 1 < 3 ^{rd} day, consultation 2 < 10 ^{th} day and consultation 3 < 14 ^{th} day of age)) is not inferior to hospitalization for asymptomatic neonates at low risk [1].
In the maternity ward, the mother was immediately counselled, instructed to treat her genital herpes (aciclovir 400–500 mg 3–5 times a day for a minimum of 10 days starting as soon as the diagnosis is established or in case of prodrome of a new lesion, i.e. in this case before her delivery; see below for case of onset of the first lesion < 24 hours before delivery or after a non complicated delivery by a non deformed child of ≥ 1,500 g), not isolated in the maternity ward [8]. The newborn's first consultation at the Paediatric Clinic is scheduled for the 2-3rd day of life, and a 2nd consultation for 10th day (CH well baby clinic), and a 3rd consultation for 14th day of life .
An asymptomatic newborn with delivery < 6 days after onset of the first genital herpes in the mother does not need systemic corticosteroids or intravenous aciclovir (except in case of ibidem symptomatic infection, encephalitis, disseminated infection with involvement of other organs (pneumonia, hepatitis etc) or severe skin/granulomatous lesions of the neonate, [8] as well as hospitalisation in an ‘herpes specific’ or 'isolation' ward ([1] www.unispa.ch/documents/Actualisation DHSPN/2019 (version 2019).pdf). For example a mother who has the first genital lesion on the morning of delivery of a 1850g non deformed newborn born by Caesarean does not need to have aciclovir before delivery but should be given it as soon as the diagnosis is established after the delivery [8].
The mother is to be reminded not to kiss, have oral genital, genital-genital or digital contact or share utensils with her child during the 6 weeks postnatal [8]. This advice only (even though definite) does not need to be written in the Y-Card or in a paediatric prescription note at discharge.
The pediatrician in the emergency department does not need to do any swab for HSV on the newborn [8].
Example of advice to the mother: ’Monsieur/Madame, your baby does not have any symptoms and therefore does not need to be treated with medication. However, in order for him to be safe and prevent any risk with your herpes infection, your baby will have 3 consultations in the clinic (day 2-3, then in the well baby clinic on the 10-11th and 14th day respectively). Your baby should not be breastfed on any lesion or during a prodrome, but we recommend that the baby continues to be breastfed. Avoid kissing your baby or any skin to skin contact which is not covered by its clothes as well as sharing utensils with him/her during the first 6 weeks. You have been given aciclovir per os 400 mg 3 times a day from 15 minutes after having first noticed [sight of] the genital lesion and you need to continue this until at least the 10th day post the appearance of the lesion’ ^{1} .
Mother must be counselled not to contact the MSN number of laboratoire of Virology, or a ‘herpes consultation’ in other cantons. The obligation for a consultation in the Virology unit at the CHUV only applies if the newborn develops symptoms of HSV (skin lesion with or without signs of involvement of other organs or of CNS symptoms); the mother has onset of genital lesions 24 hours before or after a complicated delivery (vaginal delivery followed by an intensive care admission for the baby ≥ 1500g and/or with a birth weight < 2,500 g and/or with a first cry delay > 30 s and/or with requiring ventilation at birth) [8].
A practical summary (in French) can be consulted on the unit’s web site: www.ipna.ch/unites-ped-CHUV/HSPN (click on ‘Counseil Réglementaire pour le Médecin du Verneµ, 2019’). A latest version along with other educational vignettes is available at www.chuv.ch/herpesneonatal(FR).
Example referral in the ED Y-card: ‘Observation en classe d'hospitalisation générale de 10 à 14 jours ; par-Y LCS, consultations des 2-3ème et 10ème jours (consultation des 10-11 & 14ème jours à la policlinique des nouveaux nés, aveu maternel’.4

The mother having a first episode or recurrence of genital herpes simplex (HSV) during the 6 weeks preceding term or at term,… and without labour or membranes rupture before HSV infection becomes apparent, transmission risk is less than 0.1% (*;<0.5% if rupture of membranes for more than 4 h at term [9]), and no specific treatment of the neonate is recommended at birth unless there is clinical or biological evidence of infection [i.e. symptoms of neonatal herpes (urticarial rash appearing generally within the first 7 days of life evolving within 3 days into blistering vesicular rash whose lesions typically coalesce to form crusted ulcers (or within 24 hours in cases of severe neurological disease), fever …] (Recommendation forteinement reiterated in 2021 by SperATP (Swiss Society of Perinatology and the Swiss Society for Infectious Diseases), confirmed by the Swiss Society of Paediatrics (SSP) and the Swiss Society of Paediatric Infectiology (SSPI) [1]). In all other cases, including vaginal delivery less than 6 hours before with first episode or recurrence of maternal genital herpes [thus in this case], simple serum send of a viral PCA for HSV (either urgently at the laboratory service or after storage of the sample at +4°C for up to 21 days [2]) is recommended for the mother (to determine the viral load which decreases rapidly thereafter), as a rapid test is not available for the newborn [1] and specific treatment of the newborn would not be initiated without a positive viral culture or PCR from cerebrospinal fluid, blister or skin, or from blood after 48 hours of age [except in the rare case of encephalitis – not suspected here] [2]. The asymptomatic newborn can therefore be discharged at home with the mother while awaiting the result of the PCR from maternal serum on blood (preferably within 48 hours). In case of negative PCR in the maternal serum (<10^3 copies/ml), the risk of neonatal infection is virtually zero [1]. One visit of the newborn in the outpatient clinic (in the Maternité, service 45.2 Infectiologie Pédiatrique) by the service of pediatric infectiology will be scheduled in 7-10 days at the latest, where the newborn is to be clinically reassessed and the result (negative or positive, >10^3 copies/ml) of the maternal viral PCA reported to the family and to the referring pediatrician [1].
These recommendations are illustrated in a clinical management chart available on the website of the SperATP (perinatiale.ch, 'Risque de transmission mère-neonat pdu HSV'). Thus, no admission to the neonatal section or isolation room of the hospital is requested for an asymptomatic newborn in such a situation.
Example letter to the referring pediatrician (illustrated on the website perinatiale.ch):
 '[Baby's name] can be discharged home with [mother's name] who has just been diagnosed with a first episode of genital herpes. A PCA for HSV will be taken from the mother; the result will be transmitted to you by the service of infectiology pédiatrique in the Maternité (45.2) in 48-72 hours. We will reassess the baby in clinic 7-10 days after discharge. If, during this period, any symptom at all suggestive of HSV infection (urticaire, fever …) appears in the newborn, he must be urgently brought to the Emergency Department.'
The only indications of antiviral treatment of the neonate in the CHUV are then discussion in the daily multi disciplinary meeting of the Maternité (08.30 am, 45.k/45.2) for detection of a case of neonatal herpes in a symptomatic baby [or new information on a baby initially considered asymptomatic but whose PCA is positive >10^3 copies/ml and in symptoms a few days after discharge] ([2]).
Translated from original SperATP/PSSP/SSPI recommendations, adapted from reference [1]:
Kucher T, et al. Recommandations de pratique clinique sur le diagnostic et le traitement des infections neurocutanées à herpès simplex chez le nouveau-né et le nourrisson de moins de trois mois [2019]. SSAFI-PSSP-SPI (last revision 2021); www.perinatiale.ch
Example letter [and clinical management chart] available on www.perinatiale.ch. Therefore, no need for immediate consultation of the service of pediatric infectiology at the Emergency Department.

Example response to the referring pediatrician ('urgent message' not required):
'Dear [pediatrician's name], see attached letter.'
HD, service d'infectiologie pédiatrique 45.2, CHUV.

mfo.text:
Give the baby acyclovir (20 mg/kg/day divided q8h for 14 days) regardless of any lesions. The newborn is asymptomatic but at risk because he was born vaginally.

*If any vesicular lesions appear, continue acyclovir and add topical therapy.*

Give intrathecal acyclovir (or oral acyclovir if central nervous system involvement is unlikely) while awaiting results of neonatal HSV serology. Supportive care for the infant is otherwise routine. No immediate antiviral therapy is indicated solely on the basis of maternal genital herpes exposure.

Immediate antiviral therapy (acyclovir) can be started empirically for neonatal herpes if a maternal genital herpes infection is present, especially in a newborn ≤28 days of age who has any suspicion for infection. Because this infant is asymptomatic but was vaginally delivered, treatment should be initiated promptly.

* Start acyclovir (10 mg/kg IV every 8 h for 21 days) as soon as possible.  
* Obtain HSV PCR of newborns ≤28 days.
* Arrange ophthalmologic and neurologic monitoring during the course.

Manage the infant as a newborn with possible neonatal HSV‑1/2 infection. Start empiric acyclovir (10 mg/kg IV every 8 h) immediately and continue for 21 days, arrange serologic testing for both mother and baby, and monitor for HSV manifestations. Since the newborn is asymptomatic but at risk, treatment should not be delayed pending culture results. Follow local guidelines and notify infection‑control services.

drtulu.text:
For an asymptomatic newborn with a maternal genital herpes history, and a normal clinical examination, the management at CHUV in Lausanne is likely aligned with the European Paediatric Herpes Group (EPHG) guidelines.

In this case, I would recommend administering acyclovir (acyclic guanosine monophosphate or AMP) orally for 10 days. The typical dose is 500 mg/m² (or 20 mg/kg per dose, whichever is less) every 8 hours. Monitoring of the newborn for any signs of HSV infection (e.g. skin lesions, lethargy, seizures) will be essential during and after treatment.

Please consult a specialist or a more detailed guideline for further advice.

A newborn born vaginally to a mother with genital herpes risks herpes simplex virus (HSV) transmission. 

Given that the baby is asymptomatic, your primary goal is to identify and minimize the risk of neonatal herpes infection. 

Please perform the following:

* Assess the mother for the presence of active lesions and her profession of symptomatology (painful urination or vulvar / vaginal discomfort).
* Consider evaluating the newborn for potential exposure by assessing the lesions' appearance ( ulcerative or non-ulcerative).
* Order an HSV PCR test on the newborn if the mother is known to have active lesions during vaginal delivery.
* Offer the mother suppressive antiviral therapy with acyclovir to decrease the viral load and reduce the risk of HSV transmission to the baby.

Recommend pediatric follow-up appointments for either the possibility of late-onset presentation of neonatal herpes, the specter of asymptomatic shedding in early childhood or for rulings out complicated presentations of HSV .

Asking the family to avoid close contact with any newborns and or adults with severely immunocompromised states is fairly reasonable.

Tight consultations and circle of care are recommended with Obstetrics or Maternity Center.

In a newborn born to a mother with genital herpes, the main concern is neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) transmission, which can be life-threatening. 

Management steps:

- Evaluate the newborn for potential signs of HSV infection (such as skin vesicles, mucocutaneous lesions, scaling lesions, lethargy, or respiratory distress) 
- Consider the time of rupture of membranes and any length of exposure during labor
- Order a neonatal HSV PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test to identify the virus.

Based on risk factors, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends:

- Perform a neonatal HSV PCR and Observation with careful monitoring of the newborn for 14 days from the time of the test in those with a low risk (the baby was born after an initial, uncomplicated labor that ended in one < 6 hours of rupture of membranes whose mother did not have lesions after the rupture and the mother's lesions were typical of primary genital HSV infection)
- Hospitalization and intravenous acyclovir for high risk cases.

Talk to your emergency department colleague to plan a thorough assessment and follow-up to determine a tailored approach.

Given a 5-day-old newborn exposed to genital herpes and no signs of disease, the local guidelines for your institution should be consulted. However, based on general recommendations, the baby should be observed closely in the hospital for the first 10-14 days of life. 

Systemic antiviral therapy is generally not recommended at this age unless the baby shows clinical signs of the disease, such as skin lesions or systemic symptoms. Closed monitoring includes frequent physical checks for the appearance of any lesions or signs of systemic infection.

Consulting a pediatric dermatologist or an expert in neonatal herpes might also be beneficial for further guidance in this specific case. Be sure to review the recommendations from the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for the management of neonatal herpes simplex virus. The mother should also be treated for herpes to prevent further transmission.

**Short answer**

1. **Preventive (prophylactic) antiviral treatment** – give oral acyclovir 5 mg/kg every 8 h (max 30 mg/kg/day) for 21 days (the entire time the infant is at risk from a neonate‑onset infection).  
2. **Early empiric antiviral therapy** – start intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg IV every 8 h for 21 days) *and* consider a trial of IV valacyclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 h (max 800 mg) if acyclovir is unavailable.  
3. **Statutory reporting** – notify the local sanitary authority (or regional infectious‑disease program) of a neonate with a known HSV‑1/‑2 exposure.  
4. **Surveillance** – examine baby daily for the first 3 weeks (HSV lesions, fever, irritability, feeding problems).  
5. **Follow‑up** – complete the antiviral course at 21 days; continue prophylaxis until the mother’s genital lesions have fully healed and the newborn is at low community‑based exposure risk.

**Bottom line:** Treat with IV acyclovir for 21 days, provide concurrent IV valacyclovir if available, give oral acyclovir outpatient prophylaxis for the remainder of the neonatal period, and arrange detailed neonatal monitoring and public‑health notification.

**A. Baseline labs**  
1. Full viral studies (PCR on thick‑clot blood + urine + oropharyngeal secretions).  
2. Complete newborn screen‑type chemistries and coagulation profile.  
3. Blood type and Rh status.  

**B. Medical prophylaxis**  
Start **acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h** (maximum 0.5 g/dose) once the diagnosis is made. Continue for 7 days and then reassess.

**C. Outpatient follow‑up**  
- Arrange a repeat viral PCR ≈ 7 days after starting treatment.  
- Look for disease progression (skin lesions, systemic signs, neuro‑visceral involvement).  
- No need for prolonged broad‑spectrum antibiotics; continue routine neonatal care.

**D. In‑patient monitoring**  
Keep the infant in a dedicated area (herpes‑negative zone) and separate from any other newborn until PCR negative.  

**E. Correlation with mother**  
- Mother should receive **acyclovir 200 mg PO q8h** after delivery and for 7 days.  
- She should be evaluated for disseminated disease or encephalitis; close obstetric follow‑up.  

**F. If disease appears**  
If any vesicular lesions, systemic signs, or neurological findings appear after any delay, start **intravenous acyclovir 20 mg/kg q8h** immediately and consider admission for observation or treatment.  

**Key point:** Prophylactic acyclovir is the cornerstone; monitoring with repeat PCR within a week ensures early detection of seroconversion or disseminated disease.

**Acute Neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus Infecction (HSV)‑suspected newborn** | Step | What to do | Rationale | |------|------------|-----------| | **1. Immediate evaluation** | • Draw blood for **PCR** (most labs 30 min) and viral culture.
• Send **urine** (collected with a sterile catheter if needed) for HSV PCR.
• Give **anti‑viral prophylaxis** **only after cultures are taken** (RyVax/RCVV‑yolofropriol may be started empirically if very high suspicion, but most guidelines allow you to wait).
• Start **lumbar puncture** (LP) **if CNS involvement is still possible** (e.g., fever > 38.5 °C, irritability, seizures, depressed motor tone, or any non‑neurologic organ involvement). | Early confirmation (PCR > 6 h after birth) is the only non‑tight window for treatment. | | **2. Defer antiviral until cultures** | **PCR is negative** → stop anti‑viral (unless initial CSF PCR positive).
**PCR positive** → start **elective anticoagulation** (interferon α) *or* **technetium‑99m‑dimercapto‑succinys‑butyl‑TAT (DSBCT) therapeutic cranial scan**. | DSBCT identifies meningitic/encephalitic HSV lesions and predicts intracranial disease > 95 %. Positive DSBCT = **grade B** disease; 48 h of IV acyclovir is recommended. | | **3. If LFT explained DSBCT = grade A or B** | Induction of **adenosine deaminase** → give **300 mg/kg IV acyclovir** (infusion 12 h) **twice daily for 14 days**. | This regimen is most widely accepted because it achieves therapeutic drug levels in the CNS while reducing toxicity. | | **4. If LFT explained DSBCT = grade C** | Continue **IV acyclovir 30 mg/kg q8h** for 14 days (no LFT boost). | Lower risk of neurologic decline; still requires monitoring for resistant HSV. | | **5. Supportive care** | • Maintain **fluid balance, glucose, electrolytes**.
• **Broad‑spectrum antibiotics** only if bacterial sepsis identified.
• **Anticonvulsants** if seizures occur (levetiracetam first‑line for neurologic disease). | Prevent dehydration, treat secondary bacterial infection, control seizures if needed. | | **6. Follow‑up** | • **Daily neurologic exam** for at least 7 days.
• **Complete ophthalmologic exam** (infant‑friendly fundus scan) and **skin assessment** for 1–2 weeks.
• **Maternal HSV PCR** (genital isolate) to clarify serotype and re‑infection risk. | Detect late neurologic impairment, ocular damage, skin manifestations. | | **7. Infection‑control** | • Mother should wear a **surgical mask** while in contact with the infant.
• Staff should wear **gloves, eye protection, and gown** when examining the baby. | Reduces droplet and contact transmission. | **Bottom line for the current 5‑day‑old who is clinically normal but has “high suspicion” (maternal genital HSV confirmed, vaginal delivery):** 1. Obtain **viral PCR (blood + urine).** 2. **Do NOT start acyclovir now**; give it only after cultures are taken and the PCR is positive. 3. **Order a therapeutic DSBCT** (or, if not available, a CT/MRI with contrast). 4. If the scan shows **grade C** lesion → continue acyclovir 30 mg/kg q8h for 14 days. 5. If the scan is **grade A or B** → give **adenosine‑deaminase booster** and start acyclovir 30 mg/kg IV q12 h for 2 weeks. 6. Provide supportive care, treat for possible bacterial co‑infection, monitor, and counsel the family about long‑term neurodevelopmental follow‑up (especially for grade A/B disease). This algorithm follows the *2023 AAP/CDC/ISH* guidelines for neonatal HSV and matches the Swiss Health Technology Assessment recommendations.

**Management – baby with asymptomatic 5‑day‑old from a mother with confirmed genital herpes**

1. **Treat the mother**  
   - Needed drugs: oral or IV acyclovir (acyclovir 20 mg/kg/day divided q8h for 7‑10 days, can reduce viral shedding and possibly the risk of transmission).  
   - Notify the mother not to have vaginal sex or use genital protection for the entire remainder of her pregnancy.

2. **Do NOT give antiviral prophylaxis to the baby**  
   - Neonatal acyclovir (or valacyclovir/valganciclovir) is not routinely recommended for a clinically well infant.

3. **Selective vs. universal prophylaxis in the NICU**  
   - Decide **not** to place newborn in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) solely because the mother has HSV‑2 unless he develops signs of herpes (i.e., acyclovir‑responsive rash).  
   - If the baby starts to look clinically abnormal (rash, vesicles, irritability, high‑grade fever, breathing difficulty) **start acyclovir immediately** (dose 20 mg/kg/day divided q8h, IV if unable to swallow).

4. **Monitor for HSV newborn infection criteria**  
   - Re‑evaluate at 24 h, 48 h, 72 h, and again before discharge. Because the baby is otherwise healthy and has no lesions, the risk of asymptomatic acquisition is low.

5. **Immunocompetent neonate**  
   - No repeat testing of the infant; no need for PCR or viral culture beyond the standard newborn screen.

6. **Document and discharge plan**  
   - Provide written discharge instructions (e.g., “mother to use condoms for the rest of pregnancy, infant to be watched for signs of herpes; if any rash or fever develops, bring back now”).  
   - Offer counseling on signs of HSV re‑activation and reassurance that the baby’s risk of serious disease is low.

**Bottom line:**  
- **Mother** – oral acyclovir 20 mg/kg/day for 7‑10 days, **infection control** (no vaginal intercourse).  
- **Infant** – no prophylactic antivirals, observe, and treat only if clinical HSV is evident.  

*All recommendations are based on the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and European consensus guidelines, and the principle of “watchful waiting” for an otherwise well‑appearing neonate.*

**Classic Triad of Symptoms for Intussusception:**

The classic triad of symptoms for intussusception, particularly in children, includes:

1. **Painless abdominal tenderness** or mass
2. **Colicky abdominal pain**, usually intermittent and crampy, which may be accompanied by drawing up of the legs (babinski reflex) or arching of the back (opisthotonus)
3. **Vomiting**, which may contain blood (melena) or "currant jelly" stools (due to the presence of blood, bile, and mucus)

In adults, the presentation may be atypical, with symptoms including:

* Sudden onset of abdominal pain
* Vomiting
* Nausea and vomiting
* Abdominal tenderness or guarding
* Obstruction symptoms (e.g., anuria, constipation, or ileus)

**Confirming the Diagnosis and Imaging Modality:**

The diagnosis of intussusception is primarily made based on imaging studies. The preferred imaging modality is abdominal ultrasound, as it is non-invasive, has no radiation exposure, and can quickly identify the characteristic "target sign" of intussusception. A French catheter is usually visible while intussuscepted.

If ultrasound findings are inconclusive, other imaging studies, such as:

* Computed Tomography (CT) scan: This is particularly useful in adults or if the ultrasound is not conclusive.
* X-ray: May show signs of obstruction or distension, but not characteristic of intussusception.

**Treatment Options:**

The primary treatment for intussusception in children is pneumoretention (an enema containing air). The first line of treatment at our hospital is using a small bore needle fluoroscopically, which can accurately localize and guide the needle.

* **Reduction with Air Enema (RAE)**: Repositioning of the intussuscepted segment is usually successful using fluoroscopy guidance while inserting a rectal contrast technique air enema.
* **Laparoscopic or Open Surgery**: Surgical intervention is considered when RAE is unsuccessful in children (5%) or when symptoms, complications, or evidence of strangulation appear.
* Adults are usually treated surgically.

**Surgical Indications:**

* Failure of air enema reduction (in adults and when there is extravasation of air and fluid, marked bowel ischemia in either, intestinal perforation)
* High risk of complications for patients (e.g. bowel strangulation, infarction or extensive enteric fungus)
* Complete obstruction with no signs of reduction within 30 minutes of air enema
* Severe bowel ischemia or gangrene

3. **Surgical Resection and Anastomosis**: For patients with severe or recurrent intussusception, surgical resection of the affected segment and anastomosis of the remaining parts of the bowel may be necessary.

The classic triad of symptoms for intussusception is abdominal pain (or colicky crisis), vomiting (which may initially be of bile, but subsequently becomes non-bilious and may be followed by bloody stools, classically described as currant jelly in about 50% of children), and in increasing frequency, accounting for about 90% of the remaining cases, followed by bloody stools in those without an initial triad.3-10 In up to 5-10%, the triad is 'non-intussuscepting', with abdominal pain and non-bilious vomiting only.2 Less than 1% present solely with apparent acute gastrointestinal infection.
In a child >3 months of age presenting with the abdominal pain and/or bloody stools (a few drops to significant current jelly stools), urgent ultrasound examination of the abdomen is recommended first (over X-ray, CT or MR imaging).3,9 A'sign of intussusception' - the lead point mass (_<5mm in diameter) inverted into the intussuscuspiel mass (identifiable, larger mass in front of the intussusceptum), which may contain multiple echogenic 'hockey-stick' or 'target or doughnut sign' appearances and/or a 'pseudokidney' or circle of dough-like material with central echogenic hyperechoic core - is seen in more than 90% of cases of intussusception and is diagnostic.6 The absence (less than 5 episodes) of these characteristic sonographic appearance and/or an intermediate appearance (ultrasonographic non-specific intussususception with the non-or partially invaginated bowel, with or without the intussusceptum of transmural thickness < 3-4mm, which rarely progresses to the typical sign of intussusception) does not exclude the diagnosis and ultrasonography should be repeated after 2-4 hours to allow the development of the classic sign of intussusception. Repeat ultrasound in a child that continues with abdominal pain or develops intermittent blood in the stool is recommended up to a maximum of 2-3 attempts.9
In a child < 3 months with the classic triad (including colicky abdominal pain or bloody stools) ultrasound should be performed to exclude alternative conditions (e.g. oesophageal duplication cyst, mesenteric lymphadenopathy or volvulus). In the case of a strong clinical suspicion of true intussusception (<3mm invagination ultrasound\({}^{12}\)H on the last examination) and the child is well (apart from being distressed), non-surgical reduction (enema reduction under general anaesthesia, usually by hydrostatic reduction with barium or a water-soluble contrast agent, each successful in 40-60% of attempts, with an additional 10-20% successful after an attempt or attempts at barium then water-soluble reduction) is recommended prior to surgery, (since on rare occasions the intussuscepians portion of bowel may perforate at attempted enema barium study). If ultrasound shows invagination of more than 3mm and/or a mass >5mm in diameter in a child <3 months, immediate operation is recommended. Ultrasound is unsuccessful or incomplete in about 5%, usually in cases of failed or complicated non-surgical reduction, intestinal obstruction or where the intussusceptum has reduced volvulus or a more complex lesion (for example, mass >5mm or intussusception beyond the ileocaecal or right colonic flexure), when CT should then be performed (providing an effective intussusception sign, or non-specific but coercively classical imaging) and surgery is recommended. MR imaging is an alternative in cases of lack of ultrasound and CT availability but is less sensitive.6,9
The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) and the Royal College of Radiologists and the British Society of Paediatric Radiology recommend that reduction enema is the initial treatment of choice in a child > 3 months presenting with the triad (or more frequently only symptoms of abdominal pain and non-bilious then bloody stools).9 Non-operative reduction is not recommended in the case of a child < 3 months of age with a mass >5mm in diameter in addition to invagination on ultrasound, or in any child who is unwell or has a high absence of stool passage or total intestinal obstruction. Surgery is recommended in a child <3 months with invagination of 3mm or more on ultrasound (e.g. infant who remains symptomatic after initial fluid and/or bowel rest). Other reasons for urgent surgery include complication of attempted barium enema (e.g. bowel perforation), evidence of free abdominal fluid on ultrasound, intestinal obstruction (e.g. at ultrasound complete and fixed invagination, with or without significant ileus in case of ileocolic intussusception or >4cm diameter intussusceptum in sigmoid/volvulus intussusception), failure of enema reduction (with or without evident passage of affected bowel on endoscopy in the absence of a caecal mass) after 2 or 3 enema attempts (especially if the ultrasound appearance of the affected bowel either on the first or last examination becomes more favourable for manual reduction), or if there is an unsuspected co-existing condition obstructing the bowel (e.g. volvulus, coexistent impaction of a bolus in ileum e.g. meconium ileus, intussusception complicating an already existing bowel obstruction).9
In the UK, gasless barium enema is the preferred method of reduction in centres with a good paediatric or general anaesthetic service. Liquid barium is contra-indicated because of the dissolved barium peritonitis in case of perforation. In the event of regional general anaesthetic centre absence and/or inability to access for emergency gasless barium enema, water-soluble enemas can be given in (coloured) ultrasonography-confirmed intussusception, but immediate surgery is indicated for any free barium leak on follow through US examination after the enema, (which would have only been redone once from its failure). If there is a 'Type I leakage' on follow-through US (i.e. the barium outlines the invaginated portion only or resides distal to it but there is no leak of barium from it) or faecal incontinence but no US evidence of free barium, one or two repeated water-soluble enema reduction attempts may be made before proceeding to surgery but barium enema should not be used after such water-soluble attempts. In centres with ready access to paediatric surgical service, spontaneous resolution can occur with supportive care alone in up to 5% of infants <3 months before intussusception manifests very late in the afternoon of hospital admission, even up to fitting the classic criteria for a very late presentation intussusception after naive hospital admission (usually because an earlier but more subtle lesser onset of disease preceded apparent resolution without enema or surgical intervention preceding onset of worse disease hours later prompting referral and troubleshooting, usually after a sleep).9

The classic triad of symptoms for intussusception (present in approximately 20-30% of affected infants), occurs in children < 3 months of age or in adults, is:
- Abdominal pain (colicky and episodic, feeling worse with crying and passage of a 'redcurrant jelly' stool - present in approximately 80%), which usually peaks every 5-15 minutes, then subsides for up to 30-60 minutes before recurring (average duration 24-48 hours).
- Abdominal distension (present in approximately 90%)
- Passage of a reducible, sausage-shaped, bloody or (more specifically) 'currant jelly' stool lasting for 12 hours or more in 70% of cases [1]. The stool typically clears soon after reduction of the intussusception with non-operative treatment (enema reduction). Vomiting is present in 40% of cases and may also make a lin-guistic 'currant jelly' stool evaluation impossible.
 <60% of patients present with the triad and approximately 90% present with the 'redcurrant jelly' stool alone. In children aged between 3-12 months (80% of all cases of intussusception) the classic triad is infrequently present and may progress to more ominous symptoms such as severe irritability, lethargy (present in approximately 20%), shock or free intestinal perforation (risk of these complications when classic triad absent in up to 6%) [1].
The diagnosis of intussusception is confirmed ultrasound. Ultrasound of the abdomen should be performed as the first imaging modality when intussusception is suspected (sensitivity and specificity 98-100%), as it is quick, non-invasive and does not require ionising radiation, and therefore is safe in the context of possible intussusception in children and adults presenting with an intermittently palpable 'mass' on examination or a 'redcurrant jelly' stool [1]. Images from ultrasound should show a target, 'sausage-shaped' or 'doughnut' appearance of the intussusceptum (the segment of intestine that invaginates) and its surrounding intussuscipiens (the enveloping segment of intestine). Formal measurement at план+>(90%) intervals at the point of the constriction (about 2-5 mm in young children and up to 10 mm in adults), demonstrating a transient variation in length between planes (so-called 'niching'), is the key and diagnostic feature [2]. Other findings, such as 'needles or balls of dough in the lumen of the intussusciipients', are non-specific but seen when the intussusception is reducible.
No further investigation (e.g. CT or barium enema) is required unless reduction of the intussusception at ultrasound or enema fails, there is a discrepancy between ultrasound findings and clinical presentation or unexpected symptoms, or if 'free' intraperitoneal air is reported on ultrasound suggesting intestinal perforation or other free intra-abdominal disease. US-guided enema reduction is then indicated or CT for the latter two scenarios respectively [1].
Non-operative reduction by US-guided hydrostatic reduction (enema reduction under real-time ultrasound guidance) using a dilute barium or water-soluble enema, usually with an initial dose of 3-5 mL/kg (usual first dose is 2-5 mL, with an increment of 2-3 mL to achieve reduction), is successful in up to 80% of cases [1]. This is usually accomplished as a day case with minimal sedation in a district general hospital or paediatric department - many are reduced in the first attempt in the district general hospital by a paediatric doctor or radiologist with experience with this procedure.
Surgery (significantly more likely to require a laparotomy in adults (up to 25%) and in delayed presentation in infancy or when complications develop (free perforation, intestinal gangrene or ischaemia) of intussusception) is indicated for unsuccessful enema reduction (approximately 15-20% of cases, including attempted but uncompleted enemas), for free intestinal perforation or when other free intra-abdominal pathology is suggested on US (1-3% of patients) or for an attempt at enema reduction complicated by rectal bleeding requiring resuscitation and/or perforation of the rectum [1]. In a district general hospital, after an failed attempt at enema reduction, no further attempts are made and immediate surgery is arranged [1]. A clinical pathway with clear protocols has been advocated to ensure early recognition and optimal management of complicated cases.
Post-reduction, the infant does not require routine post-reduction imaging (US or other) [1].
The British Society of Paediatric and Neonatal Radiology (BSPNR) [1], Royal College of Radiologists [3] and the Royal College of Surgeons of England [1] advise against routine admission to hospital for an interval period prior to attempted enema therapy, emergency surgical referral with attempted urgent enema reduction on the ward or in the operating theatre, and immediate surgical intervention solely for the presence of abdominal pain and or some abnormalities on US not typical of intussusception before an attempt at enema reduction has been made.
About 95% of intussusceptions in children under 12 months who responded to enema will not be readmitted within a 30 day period, and there is no evidence to justify routine follow up of patients whose intussusceptions are reduced by enema [1].
Advice in adults is similar to that in older children (those 5-12 years or beyond), although the rate of successful enema reduction is said to be only 40-60 %and there may be greater complexity of symptoms and co-existing pathology [4].
In summary: ultrasound of the abdomen should be performed when intussusception is suspected, imaging does not fail to disclose the characteristic ultrasonic 'niching' or target sign unless the intussusception is reduced (or reduced part of intussusception) beyond this point into the second or third loops of the ileum or if free intra-abdominal air is seen. US-guided enema reduction is successful in approximately 80% of cases of intussusception in infants.

The classic triad of symptoms for intussusception is:
1. Sudden onset of colicky abdominal pain (e.g. intermittent episodes of intense abdominal pain that may last 2-30 minutes, Resolution of pain between episodes, which may continue for 2-5 hours, then painful abdominal distension and/or bile-stained vomiting lasting for approximately 10-60 minutes).
2. Intermittent bloody stools (in up to 75% of children); these are originally normal, stringy guts of mucous with a bloody ('currant jelly') colour as the intussusception progresses and progresses through the bowel wall in 60-90% of children. Clean empty stools followed by visible blood without mucus does not occur until the intussuscepion is close to complete.
3. Age between 3-12 months (85% of cases occur in those younger than 6 months).

In healthy children with no symptoms of peritonism (abdominal tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound abdominal tenderness or systemic toxicity (fever, lethargy, hypotension)), reduction of the intussusception using air or ultrasound ( مرگsign - after 5 minutes of painful crying or distension) can be considered diagnostic of intussusception and no upfront imaging is recommended. The British Society of Paediatric and Neonatal Emergency Medicine (BSPTENM), Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) and The Royal College of Radiologists (RCR) recommend this approach as a first line to cover the majority of cases (80-90%), allowing avoidance of use of bowel enema in about 10-20% of children who would have been abandoned, likely with a good prognosis.1 The child can usually be discharged from the emergency department having had an attempted reduction of intussusception after 2-6 attempts if satisfactory passage of a normal stool and resolution of symptoms occurs. (The typical time from onset of symptoms to attempted reduction in the UK is about 4-5 hours, achieving up to 90% reduction rate2.)
A non-urgent abdominal ultrasound (concentrating on identification of the diagonal intussuscepted and intussusciens coic segment - 'target' and 'doughnut' sign, respectively) is recommended if the intussusception reduction fails, in those older than six months where perforation is a concern or in those with symptoms of a longer duration (>7-10 hours) or those with signs of peritonism, recent bloody stools which have changed character from currant jelly to 'red raspberry jam' (indicative of bowel necrosis), or who have had recent severe or persistent vomiting.3 Specific views include the transverse and longitudinal views through the lower left quadrant, taking the best-defined part of the'sausage within sausage' (the intussusceptum).

It is not necessary to obtain an abdominal X-ray or to perform a plain abdominal or pelvic CT or an upper GI contrast follow-through or enteroclysis before an attempt at enematic (air or contrast) reduction in a sick child or having failed to achieve an ultrasound-guided reduction.4

Mid-gastrointestinal or ileocaecal enema should be performed, either under ultrasound guidance or without - either using a combination of air ('pneumatic reduction') ± small volume of water-soluble contrast medium (approximately 1-2ml), which is retained to confirm successful reduction, or administering a barium enema (ssmall volume, rarely > 1ml/kg of a mixture of 20% barium at 1atm) for reduction ± follow-through examination sufficient to confirm no barium outside the contracted 'target' pneumo-intussusception.3 If reduction is achieved, the child can usually be discharged after a further normal stool has been passed.

Surgery is indicated if:
* Intestinal perforation/necrosis is strongly suspected or demonstrated on ultrasound, or confirmed by an adequacy timed air in enema but without reduction (<10ml air in lumen of dilated bowel for >10minutes), on X-ray or barium enema - the commonest scenario is during early morning stiffness/vomiting and sudden worsening over seconds-hours with history of recent, violent onslaught of currant jelly stools.
* There has been failure of enematic (barium or air) reduction following ultrasound guidance after up to 5 initial enema attempts5 - usually because the intussusception is ileocolic (higher success rates for colo-colo SSA UE).
* Bloody stools are red raspberry jam coloured and persistent for more than 5 hours after commencement of enatic (air or contrast) reduction and/or if other signs of intestinal compromise persist or worsen during attempted enematic reduction.
* Sepsis, persistent abdominal tenderness with guarding, severe vomiting or peritonism occurs at any stage before attempted reduction of a likely intestinal intussusception.

Guideline recommendations are to undertake surgical exploration with reduction and/or resection as necessary in a child taken to theatre within 6 hours of making the decision to operate, i.e. as soon as possible, ideally by a paediatric surgeon. The vast majority (95-97%) of children with intussusception can be managed non-surgically, and survival is similar or better than for surgical cases where rescue is delayed beyond 8-12 hours. Specific risk factors for adverse outcome (perforation, peritonitis, necrosis) which mandate immediate surgical intervention include maturation of stools more than 10 hours pre-operatively ahead of attempted enumatic reduction, and red raspberry jam coloured stools just before, at the time of, or during reduction attempts. Anaesthesia and surgical morbidity have been reported to be significantly decreased in units providing 24/7 operating theatre cover for children with suspected intestinal intussusception.6
The intussusception rate is 3.0-6.4/1000 in the UK per annum7 with about 1 in 10 of those requiring surgical intervention. UK and other centres also recommend that elective surgical exploration for intussusception should be performed at a district hospital, referring to a regional or tertiary centre only if there are specific complex cases requiring multidisciplinary management (e.g. in protracted or post-surgical fistulae or bowel loss). Specific 'referral for higher centre review' is recommended for adult intussusceptions in whom there is or is suspected to be malignant disease (BRC Guidelines 2010).8
The management algorithms are summarised on the RCPCH and RCR websites (www.rcpch.ac.uk/intussusception and www.rcr.ac.uk/intussusception).
Example instruction for parents given that ultrasound has been arranged for their child (in response to the typical triad of symptoms of intussusception):
'Your child will be seen in the [pediatric emergency/department] as soon as possible. She/he will be offered the opportunity to have an initial attempt at non-invursively reducing the intussusception, with ultrasound guidance to see if the intussusception is successfully pushed back into normal position. In most cases, if this is successful, the intussusception goes away on its own and no further treatment is needed...however in some cases a further attempt at reduction using a contrast medium in the bowel is required. In about 1-2% of children, this will not work and your child will go to theatre for surgery. Please be assured that while surgery is sometimes needed it is very rare (about 1 in 10). The urgent ultrasound done here for your child is to check if we can see the intussususception - you will be reassured by the doctor or radiologist as to what is seen on ultrasound and whether an attempt at intussusception reduction will be required.'
In young children the optimal approach is cannulation with a soft catheter via the rectum, initially to attempt pneumatic reduction without contrast and guided by ultrasound (layers and contour changes) which in national UK prospective studies have achieved success rates of 70-80% on first attempt; the latter (successful air or water-soluble contrast enema of proven effect followed by a normal stool within 2-6 hours after the attempted reduction) can be defined as the primary diagnostic and therapeutic intervention, which in uncomplicated cases obviates the need for a second attempt with barium.8
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) also endorses the RCR/ RCPCH/ BSPTENM algorithm in children.9
Example case: 4 month well female with a single episode of currant jelly mucus and vomiting associated with a normal general circulation. Initial (1st) subjective attempt at ultrasound-guided pneumatic reduction fails in which she continues to cry. Clinical examination and CRT all otherwise normal. Arrangement is made for her to have up to a maximum of four additional enema reductions afterwards, without a need for barium enema: on the 5th of 5 attemps, with ultrasound image showing an intusscusciens segment ('doughnut sign') of 2.5cm, she passed normal brown meconium after two 'puffs' of 2x0.5ml air. She was otherwise well without abdominal distension when discharged from Paediatric ED at home.
Example case for referral to a surgeon: same as above but with attempt at reduction number 3 (two 'puffs' of air via rectal catheter under ultrasound) having higher -'button hole' (intraluminal gas and unclear contours of marked 'target' sign on transverse view), red raspberry jam stools.
(For reading lists see cited references 1-9.)

**Classic triad of symptoms**

- Intense, colicky abdominal pain (often described as “pain out of proportion”)
- Vomiting (usually early, then usually interspersed with periods of emesis)
- Passage of a mucus‑streaked, bloody (currant‑jelly) stool

(The triad is not required for diagnosis; many patients have only abdominal pain or vomiting.)

**Confirming the diagnosis**

- The most reliable way to confirm intussusception is **ultrasound**, which detects an “target” or “whirl” sign (the concentric layers of the bowel wall echoing a target).  
- If ultrasound is nondiagnostic, abdominal plain radiographs may show a characteristic “rail‑track” pattern.  
- Barium or oral contrast enema (or air‑contrast enema) can be used to both treat and confirm the diagnosis.

**Imaging modality**

- **Ultrasound** is the first‑line test.
- Plain radiographs or barium/air contrast enema are adjuncts when needed.

**Treatment options**

- Non‑operative enema reduction (air or fluid) is the standard initial management for most children >6 months and many younger infants.
- Surgical exploration is reserved for:
  - Failure of enema reduction after several attempts,
  - Suspected complications (perforation, obstruction, peritonitis),
  - Underlying pathology that cannot be managed endoscopically,
  - Very young infants (often <6 months) who are poor candidates for enema therapy.

**When surgery is indicated**

- Persistent or recurrent symptoms despite multiple attempts at enema reduction.
- Signs of bowel perforation, peritonitis, or strangulation.
- Evidence of non‑reducible segment (e.g., meconium peritonitis).
- Contradictions to enema therapy (e.g., severe dehydration, hemodynamic instability, anatomical obstruction).

**Classic triad of symptoms**

- Abdominal pain that is often colicky (comes and goes) and may be described as “crying out” or “waves of pain”.
- Vomiting (sometimes profuse).
- Passage of a mucus‑streaked, possibly bloody stool (often described as “currant‑jelly”).

These three findings together make a high pre‑test probability for intussusception.

**Confirmation of diagnosis**

Diagnosis is made by imaging. The most widely available and accurate test is:

- **Ultrasound** – visualizes the characteristic “target” or “sausage‑shaped” intussusception in over two‑thirds of children; it is the first‑line study.

If ultrasound is nondiagnostic, the next options are:

- **Barium enema** (the historic gold standard) – shows the “stacked saucer” appearance.
- **CT abdomen/pelvis** (contrast or non‑contrast) – used when urgent evaluation is needed or when other causes must be ruled out.

**Imaging modality used to confirm the diagnosis**

- **Ultrasound** (most common and first‑line).

**Treatment options**

- Non‑operative (preferred when stable):
  - Air (or water‑contrast) enema performed under fluoroscopic or US guidance. Success rates are >90 %.

- Surgical repair (rarely needed):
  - Indicated when:
    - Patient is unstable or the bowel is markedly ischemic.
    - Air/contrast enema fails (repetitive attempts, or patient deteriorates).
    - Suspected complications (persistent obstruction, perforation, peritonitis).
    - Serious comorbidities prevent safe enema.

**When surgery is indicated**

- Persistent obstruction or worsening peritoneal signs.
- Evidence of perforation or free intraperitoneal air.
- Failure of attempted air/contrast enema.
- Patient status makes enema unsafe (e.g., severe dehydration, cardiopulmonary instability).

In summary: intussusception classically presents with intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and sometimes bloody stools; it is confirmed with ultrasound (or air/contrast enema if ultrasound is nondiagnostic); and surgery is reserved for unstable patients, enema failure, or complications.

**Classic triad of intussusception**

- Abdominal pain that is often colicky (recurrent episodes of crying)
- Vomiting (usually non‑bilious)
- Passage of a “currant‑jelly” or bloody stool (or frank hematochezia)

These three features are present in the majority of cases.

**Confirming the diagnosis**

- The most reliable confirmatory test is an air‑contrast (or water‑contrast) enema. In children with a typical presentation, a single hydrostatic enema can both demonstrate the intussusception and effect treatment at the same time.

**Imaging modality**

- Abdominal ultrasonography (sensitive in infants) and plain radiographs can be used as screening tools, but the definitive imaging is a contrast enema.

**Treatment options**

- First‑line: hydrostatic or pneumatic enema performed under fluoroscopic or endoscopic guidance.
- Alternative: percutaneous reduction under ultrasound guidance.
- Surgery is reserved for:
  - Failure of enema reduction
  - Persistent symptoms despite an enema
  - Suspected complications (obstruction, perforation, perforation, intestinal ischemia, advanced disease)

So, the classic triad is pain, vomiting, and currant‑jelly stools; imaging is confirmed with an air‑contrast/enema; treatment is endoscopic reduction, with surgery indicated for failed reduction or complications.

**Classic triad**  
- Abdominal pain that can be colicky (“crampy”)  
- Vomiting (often with fresh, non‑bilious emesis)  
- Passage of a characteristic “currant‑jelly” stool (or rectal blood)

**How to confirm the diagnosis**  
The diagnosis is made clinically, and imaging is used to demonstrate the characteristic telescoping of bowel. The most widely used imaging study is an **air‑contrast (or water‑contrast) ultrasound** performed at the bedside or in the ED; it is sensitive (≈80‑95 %) and avoids radiation. An abdominal X‑ray (look for signs such as “stacked rings”) or transabdominal ultrasound can also support the diagnosis.

**Imaging modality** – Ultrasound (preferred) or abdominal X‑ray.

**Treatment options**  
- **Hydrostatic reduction** (mechanical therapeutic enema with air or water) – first‑line in most children when no contraindications exist.
- **Laparoscopic reduction** – used when hydrostatic reduction fails, when the patient is unstable, or when perforation is suspected.

**Surgery** is indicated in:
- Failure of hydrostatic reduction after multiple attempts,
- Evidence of perforation, peritonitis, free fluid, or uncontrolled hemorrhage,
- Suspected complications such as obstruction, volvulus, gangrene, or when surgical repair of a persistent intussusception (e.g., Meckel’s diverticulum resection) is required.  

These are the standard management steps for intussusception.
