drtulu.text:
The cardinal or 'key' characteristic symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) are: (a) rest tremor in one or more limbs (usually an asymmetrical, action (or postural) tremor of a 'pill-rolling' type, typically affecting the hands), (b) bradykinesia (reduced voluntary movement of the limbs, slowness of movement) and/or (c) rigidity (increased resistance to passive movement). Applying a simple challenge task to the patient (such as opening a caught grasp or standing up from a chair) usually brings out both bradykinesia/rigidity (and often the tremor) in a more obvious way than having the patient just sit still or lie at rest.

The other major group of symptoms (the 'parkinsonism equivalent' but predominantly non-motor symptoms in PD) may precede or develop shortly after the onset of these cardinal motor symptoms. These include: (d) impaired postural stability with a tendency to postural instability (a late feature in the disease); (e) micrographia (small handwriting); and (f) decreased spontaneous movement of facial and other muscles (hypomimia).

Non-motor symptoms such as fatigue, apathy, and autonomic dysfunction (including constipation, urinary frequency, orthostatic hypotension and/or anhidrosis) and sleep disturbances are also very common in PD and may be the initial or predominant symptoms in up to 25-40% of patients. Other additional non-motor and motor features may include mood disorders (depression and anxiety), excessive daytime somnolence, mood fluctuations, and cognitive disturbances (mild cognitive impairment to dementia in a minority). This wide range of possible presentations in a single patient makes diagnosis, particularly at the very early stages of the disease, not always straightforward.

Not all patients who develop tremor, at least of 'parkinsonian type', have PD - a number will have essential tremor (which is a much more common disorder). A diagnosis of PD should not be made based solely on the presence of parkinsonian tremor, particularly in the absence of bradykinesia/akinesia and/or rigidity (and preferably in the absence of both of these key features). Rigidity is always present when the tremor is present at rest in PD, whereas in essential tremor, the tremor is never present at rest (it usually appears on action and/or postural challenge and may abate when the limb is at rest).

Formal diagnostic criteria have been published to improve diagnostic accuracy and to allow distinction between PD and other causes of parkinsonism. A clinical diagnosis of PD is typically made when a patient has at least two of the three cardinal motor features (rest tremor, bradykinesia/rigidity), for at least three months, in the presence of an 'excluded alternate diagnosis' such as secondary parkinsonism due to brain injury, toxin, metabolite disorder, drug or infection. More detailed guidance and diagnostic 'red flags' for atypical parkinsonism (which including syndromes such as progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy and corticobasal degeneration, where an atypical response to levodopa and different disease course may be expected) are given by the Royal College of Physicians Clinical Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of PD in 2017, although not reproduced here [1]. The 'three month rule' acknowledges that bradykinesia or rigidity alone may be present for short periods ('benign akinesia' or 'benign akathisia') and PD is subsequently diagnosed if full-blown parkinsonism develops on follow-up.
Box 1 provides an example of how a clinical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease can be made (or alternatively, other parkinsonism judged to be likely or highly probable PD excluded on a predefined basis).

Box 1.
[LLU example]:
52-year-old woman with postural instability and self-reported slight slowness of walking. She has been noticed to write in a fine, diminished handwriting script over the past six months. She does not have a tremor of her hand at rest but becomes aware of a kinetic tremor (tremor on movement or arrest in movement that worsens with a skilled task such as writing, pouring tea, etc) during activities. Her medications have not changed, including paroxetine started 12 months ago for endogenous depression.

On examination bradykinesia and slight asymmetrical postural instability are present and micrographia demonstrated; minimal tremor (predominantly kinetic), unaffected face or other limbs. She is independent in ADLs, MMSE is 29/30. Haemoglobin 9.1, serum urea and electrolytes were normal.

_FOLLOWING THE RULE OUT OF ALTERNATE DIAGNOSES BY HISTORY, MEDICAL EXAMINATION AND AS NEEDED BY INVESTIGATIONS (such as blood tests for chronic kidney disease and thyroid function tests -the latter particularly if her symptoms initially improved when on paroxetine - or when she has hypotension, unexplained weight loss or constipation unexplained by age and sex as she is otherwise well), a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease is made on the basis of the presence of: bradykinesia, postural instability and micrographia, over 3 months. The kinetic tremor in keeping with PD, especially since there is no rest tremor. The response to 'challenge with a skilled task' such as writing clearly brings out the kinetic tremor_

In contrast:
A 62-year-old man with 3 month history of rest tremor in his right hand, subtle 'fidgeting' of this hand for the first time and slightly more efficient walking speed thanpreviously. Normal blood results (thyroid and renal function tests), plasma homovanillic acid (HVA), normal MMSE score. There is no evidence of bradykinesia or rigidity in a limb.

In this case, a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease is not made: the absence of cardinal motor symptoms of PD (bradykinesia/rigidity) despite rest tremor in one limb is consistent with a diagnosis of essential tremor.

It is only around 4-5 years after an initial presentation with tremor alone that a significant proportion of patients so diagnosed develop the other two cardinal symptoms of PD and/or dementia.

The estimation of 4-5 years to the development of full-blown parkinsonism or significant learned disability in the ability to perform daily tasks ('Parkinson's disease with tremor only at onset') is used to reliably discriminate PD from essential tremor; a minority of cases of PD in the elderly may also begin purely as tremor (known as 'delayed PD onset') [2].

Other investigation (such as MRI brain or dopamine transporter imaging with DAT scans) is not necessary in the early evaluation of PD or for diagnostic classification and is not recommended according to the Royal College of Physicians guidelines [1]. It is only used in diagnostic difficulty or uncertainty regarding the subtype of parkinsonism when a neurological condition with a potential different therapeutic target and/or prognosis (such as multiple system atrophy, Parkinson's disease with dementia or progressive supranuclear palsy) is suspected and in cases where dopatherapy or deep brain stimulation is to be initiated early (within 12-18 months of onset and predominantly after a poor response to 4-6 weeks of levodopa and other dopaminergic agents).

Examples of unusual or atypical initial presentations of PD, which in the absence of further symptoms need no immediate imaging or search for further pathology, include the following:
* Diaphoresis or excessive salivation, prolonged unexplained sleep periods, rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) [in the absence of other strongly suggestive symptoms, such as seizures or abnormal jerks], orthostatic hypotension or constipation.
* And, importantly, more complex patterns such as prominent gait disturbance without tremor several weeks before slow limbs appear, with the formerly additionally absent cardinal features of PD emerging in months.

The three main characteristic or cardinal and most disabling motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) are:

* Tremor (usually a resting tremor of a limb, most commonly the hand (186-71% of patients), less often the foot (15-30%) or less frequently the head or mouth), persisting as long as the limb is at rest and ceasing or diminishing when the limb is lifted or purposefully moved.
* Bradykinesia (or hypokinesia) - slowness of movement and/or muscle constraint, resulting in difficulties with initiating, execution or speed of voluntary movements (95-100% of patients).
* Rigidity - an increased tone or stiffness of the limb or trunk that is present at rest (or more pronounced with passive movement) and is typically described as lead-pipe or cogwheel in quality (90-98% of patients). Cogwheel rigidity is a ratchety or 'catch and release' feeling on passive movement of the limb, usually first detected in the arm, associated with a focal increase in muscle tone resistant to passive movement, but not with clasp-knife spasticity (in contrast to that seen in other extrapyramidal and pyramidal disorders).

One or more of these cardinal motor features must be present for at least 3 months for a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease to be made.[1] Axial symptoms, including postural instability (impaired balance and unsteadiness, in 42-74% of patients), and gait disturbances (slow gait, short stride length and wide base of support, in 90-95%) are also common and can be disabling, but are not considered one of the three cardinal features.

The other common non-motor symptoms (present in 50-95% of patients during the disease course)[2,3] include fatigue, sleep disorders (insomnia, restless legs or REM sleep behaviour disorder), anxiety, depression (moderate to severe in 30-40% of patients) and cognitive impairment (predominantly mild non-dementia executive impairment, in 20-40%).

Extrapyramidal and other non-classical motor features are more common in early disease (such as micrographia (small handwriting), microsthatism, masked face) and can either be absent or simultaneously present with the cardinal symptoms. The presence or absence of rest tremor correlates with the likelihood of a definitive diagnosis of Parkinson's disease in a patient with parkinsonism: the absence of a rest tremor in a patient with bradykinesia and rigidity (parkinsonism without tremor) increases the likelihood of an 'atypical parkinsonian disorder' (e.g. multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy or post-encephalitic parkinsonism), with atypical parkinsonian disorders accounting for 10-20% of parkinsonism diagnoses in specialist centres.[4]

It is essential to distinguish Parkinson's disease from atypical parkinsonism, a range of neurodegenerative diseases that share some symptoms of Parkinson's disease but also have distinctive clinical features and often a more rapid progression and more prominent non-motor features (e.g. prominent autonomic dysfunction, early severe gait instability and a characteristic postural instability gait disorder with a tendency to falls, distinct speech and eye movement abnormalities).

Diagnostic criteria recommended by the UK Parkinson's disease society brain bank medical and scientific advisory board (2017) and those of the Movement Disorders Society (2017) [5,6] specify that a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease should only be made if there is a definite resting tremor, clear bradykinesia and rigidity, and preferably a smooth response to dopaminergic replacement with levodopa (and/or dopamine agonist and/or MAO-B inhibitor)[1,6]. Rigorous clinical evaluation and sometimes additional investigations, including substantial improvement in response to a dopamine test, usually lasting at least 1-2 hours with levodopa or dopamine agonist (a course of levodopa 100-200mg orally every 1-2 hours for 1-2 hours), may be required to confidently distinguish PD from atypical parkinsonism in some cases.

Examples of atypical parkinsonism which may require further investigation (e.g. brain MRI scanning with diffusion weighted and or 1Tesla FLAIR sequences in the presence of a unexplained pure gait disorder, decline or symptom evolution suggestive of early postural instability, unexplained speech or eye movement disorders, and/ or complex, early autonomic dysfunction), include multiple system atrophy (MSA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and Parkinson's disease with dementia (PDD) (where true parkinsonism has developed in a patient with pre-existing dementia).

Non-degenerative parkinsonian syndromes (such as drug-induced parkinsonism and post-anoxic parkinsonism) can also present in a variable way, sometimes indistinguishably from PD, and may require specific investigations and separation from PD, MSA or other atypical parkinsonism.
In the early stages of the disease, PD may be misdiagnosed as a benign disorder such as depression, fatigue or osteoarthritis and symptoms may be attributed to ageing.

Acase in which the initial presentation includes non-motor and non-classical motor symptoms without any or only a mild resting tremor does not automatically preclude a diagnosis of PD, particularly if the patient or patient's carer can provide a history of evolutionary gradual onset and progression of new movement symptoms over months and if there is a positive response to dopaminergic treatment.

In almost all cases of unusual presentation (e.g. a patient under the age of 50 with Parkinsonism), referral to a specialist service with experience in PD and atypical parkinsonism is recommended to ensure accurate diagnosis and avoid overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis of PD and other neurodegenerative conditions.

Boxed-example of clinical clues to help diagnosis of Parkinson's disease or an atypical parkinsonian disorder:
PD (almost always with a resting tremor) - slow onset, gradual progression of the three cardinal motor features and evolution to significant axial symptoms over >1 (to 3) years.
MSA (or other atypical parkinsonian disorder) - sudden or acute onset; prominent autonomic dysfunction at onset (sometimes or from an early stage); gait disorder/disability from an early stage or presenting as a 'falls disorder'; speech disturbances or loss of postural sense and gait ataxia etc from an early stage or within the first 2 years; unsteady gait characterised by a short or very short stride length, often with a tendency to falls; presence of ataxia e.g. intention tremor, dysmetria.
Changes in tone qualitatively different from parkinsonian rigidity (e.g clasp-knife spasticity characteristic of multiple system atrophy).

Example of a clinical algorithm for the assessment of a patient presenting with parkinsonism is provided in the 2017 guidelines of the UK Parkinson's disease society brain bank.[1, 7]

The characteristic and most common early symptoms of Parkinson disease (PD) are the 'four cardinal motor features' which account for >70-80% of patients at diagnosis [1]. These are:

1. Bradykinesia (slowness of movement) or akinesia (loss of voluntary movement). In PD this typically manifests as:
	* Micrographia (small, cramped handwriting or drawings)
	* Difficulty initiating or executing a voluntary movement (e.g. getting out of a chair, turning in bed)
	* Shortened or reduced amplitude of voluntary movements (e.g. diminished axial and limb rotation).
2. Resting tremor (typically rhythmic, utilising or 'pill-rolling', involving the fingers or hand). This is often asymmetrical and occurs at rest, disappearing with voluntary action (action myoclonus or inteference) lasting > 3 seconds [this differentiates it from 'action tremor' such as seen in essential tremor]. Less commonly, and often late in the disease, it is postural or action-based. Rest tremor in PD involves mainly the hands (the most common site), but also, less frequently, the foot, face (buccolingual tremor e.g. grasping-snatching of the lower lip), or trunk.
3. Rigidity. In PD this is lead-pipe or cogwheel in character. Lead-pipe rigidity is a progressive increase in resistance to movement in a uniform and sustained manner as in a pipe filled with lead. Cogwheel (or ratchety) rigidity is demonstrated by a jerky, ratcheting feel or 'catch-and-release' with passive movement of the limb, often with a more sudden or abrupt release.
4. Postural and gait disturbances (postural instability). This may manifest as:
	* Retropulsion (where the patient tends to fall backwards)
	* Reduced arm swing or shorter steps
	* Shuffling gait, often with a tendency to postural distortion (e.g. leaning forwards, asymmetry of posture and/or step length).

The first symptom in PD in about 50-75% of patients is a unilateral tremor, resting in character and usually of the hand [2]. Bradykinesia then develops over time, with rigidity and postural/gait disturbances appearing later, usually within 2 years of diagnosis. The cardinal symptoms may be present unilaterally, often on one side of the body, for at least 6-9 months to fulfill the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank clinical diagnostic criteria for idiopathic PD (previously known as 'probable and definite PD') [1].
Up to 50% of patients will experience one or more 'non-motor symptoms' as their first or earliest symptom(s), often of two categories:
- Autonomic symptoms (e.g. constipation, urinary urgency and frequency, excessive daytime somnolence).
- Neuropsychiatric symptoms (e.g. anxiety, depression, anxiety or depression in early morning wakening).

Motor symptoms other than the four cardinal features, such as dysphonia, sialorrhoea, ‘masked facies’ or 'frozen' shoulder, can also be present in PD at onset. These do not meet the diagnostic criteria for the cardinal features, but may be disabling or concerning and should be treated if needed.

It is worth noting that about 5-10% of patients with parkinsonian syndrome will have 'atypical-parkinsonism' (the designation of Parkinson's disease remaining for those with the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank clinical diagnostic criteria fulfilled as above). Atypical parkinsonism is less likely to have tremor (`parkinson-plus syndromes', such as MSA, PDD or PSP) or a tremor-dominant phenotype as a first symptom [3].

Boxed summary of the defining cardinal motor features of Parkinson's disease:
* Resting tremor (asymmetrical)
* Bradykinesia or akinesia
* Lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity (not leading edge rigidity in non-PD causes)
* Postural and/or gait disturbances

(Symphalphasia (difficulty speaking) at rest and/ or hypomimia (masked facies) and micrographia may often be present early or at diagnosis but they are not used as diagnostic features, being common in non-motor symptoms in both typical and atypical parkinsonism).

Early non-motor and other (axial and non-rigorous appendicular) motor symptoms may be present in PD at the time of the diagnosis and require assessment.

Diagnostic criteria for PD cannot be 'set' by a single symptom, its absence being no argument against a PD diagnosis if two of the cardinal features are present. Table 1 of the clinical criteria [1] is reproduced below:
"Determine one year ofoutine occupationally impairing parkinsonism, satisfy one of the following:
	Both A and B, or
At least two of B, C, D, B and C, or D and C
A - Reduced fluctuations in axial movements or their amplitude (akinesia or bradykinesia)
B - Resting tremor
C - Rigidity
D - Postural instability or gait
 NB A alone is insufficient,
B alone is insufficient if only an indistinct or slight ( < 6 months duration) unilateral tremor, and C or D with transient or slight (< 6 months duration) unilateral tremor".

(eg, patients with an indistinct tremor alone <6 months or postural instability alone after 6 months, do not meet criteria for PD alone).

A diagnosis of PD can be considered probable if there are two of these features in the above paragraph present together (table 1 of the PKDB criteria) or one, with clinical evidence of PD over 6 months and response to dopaminergic treatment (noting these patients would meet criteria had symptoms not stabilised over 6 months),and there are no features of other parkinsonism that along with other factors Chile oforta atypical Parkinsonian syndrome [1].

In about 5-10% of patients the diagnosis of PD will remain unfulfilled, often a wait of several years being required after initial/symptomatic assessment to fulfil diagnostic criteria.

A straightforward clinical history and examination including Parkinson's disease Society Brain Bank criteria [1] is considered the best first choice for making the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease in routine clinical practice, particularly in specialist neurology clinics [2]. A positive response (PD or improvement of parkinsonism lasting >3 months) to a trial of dopaminergic therapy e.g. levodopa or dopamine agonist ("disease-mitotic response") in a patient with 'probable' hippocampus does not in itself prove a diagnosis of PD, and the diagnosis should be reappraised relying still solely on clinical criteria after stopping these treatments [1, 4].

In contrast, the use of 'Parkinsonism elimination protocols' and extensive investigation by 'disease-localising tools' such as the UPDRS-r6 (six item score for postural instability and gait difficulty, often untypical in PD), computerised ('quantitated') imaging of the nigrostriatal dopamine pathway (e.g., DAT-SPECT) and novel genetic testing are recommended only in:
* Atypical parkinsonism syndrome or in atypical parkinsonian symptom pattern diagnosis of PD is uncertain after careful assessment with clinical criteria [1, 3].
* Young age (eg < 40 years, < 20 in familial PD)
A full explanation and discussion of the diagnostic process in these situations should be provided to the patient [4, 5].

References:
[1] Plant GT, Bain PG et al; for the Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank Criteria for Parkinson's Disease (2002-2006) [Corrected March 2017]. npj Parkinson's disease (2018); 4 :4, <https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/pdfs/PKDB_Criteria.pdf>
[2] Working Group on Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's disease; PNBS Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (2017). npj Parkinsons disease (2017); 3 :4 doi: 10.1038/s41531-017-0004-y.
[3] Lees AJ, et al. Diagnosis and treatment of progressive supranuclear palsy (NICE clinical guideline 119) [CG 119]. London: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence 2011.
[4] Fung VSC, et al, on behalf of the Working Group on Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's disease; PNBS Guidelines for the Management of Newly Diagnosed Parkinson's disease in Adults (2017). npj Parkinsons disease (2017); 3 :15 doi: 10.1038/s41531-017-0002-0, <https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/pdfs/PDN_topics_ND_guidelines_ultimate.pdf>
[5] the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines 'Parkinson's disease: diagnosis and management of Parkinson's disease in adults (NICE Clinical Guideline 82, update 2017 and re issued, final version withdrawn November 2017) at www.nice.org.uk [accessed 24 March 2019] recommended 'On an uncertain diagnosis a specialist clinic referral should be arranged to the regional PD NHS specialist centre taking a practice of repeat clinical review after 6-12 months as well as or by trying a short trial of dopaminergic therapy directly (i.e. an informal and temporary "disease-mitotic response" trial not part of any controlled trial Element)'. This was based on advice from the British Neurological Association - Expert Group on Parkinson's disease diagnosis [1].</s

The characteristic early symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) are a good 'hand-motor' or 'limb' symptom (bradykinesia and/or tremor), and often a combination of one or two others from the following categories (the 'triad' of cardinal symptoms):

1. **Bradykinesia** (slowness of movement or akinesia - difficulty initiating movement) which may manifest as:
	* Slowness or delay in initiating a movement (e.g. rising from a chair, changing position).
	* Reduced amplitude of movement (small writing or stepping movements).
	* Difficulty with rapid alternating movements (e.g. tapping both feet or fingers rapidly).
* Bradykinesia is the most disabling and earliest feature of PD in approximately 80% of patients ^{1}.
2. **Rest tremor**, typically one of the following:
	* An 'action' or 'on movement' tremor that decreases or disappears on voluntary movement (relenting tremor - e.g. a hand tremor that stops when the patient places the hand in the pocket of their coat).
	* A **rest tremor**, which is present when the limb is at rest and usually most evident in one finger (usually the thumb, middle finger or index finger) or the wrist, with a characteristic 'pill-rolling' or 'cogwheel' quality in ~70% of patients ^{2}.

Other cardinal motor symptoms may develop less commonly in the first year or so after symptom onset, contributing to the characteristic 'parkinsonian gait' (short, shuffling steps without arm swing, often with postural flexion of the trunk: the 'festinating gait'), bradyphrenia (slowness of thinking) and/or hypomimia (reduced facial expression).

Non-motor symptoms may also be present early but are not included in the diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's. These include fatigue, anxiety, constipation, sleep disturbance, difficulty with keeping track of belongings or mental tasks (cognitive features such as MILD 'executive dysfunction' and possibly slight impairment in working (short term) memory ^{1,3}.

Not all of the following characteristic Parkinson's symptoms may be present initially: postural instability (loss of balance); Levodopa-responsive akinesia-rigidity gait and rigidity without a rest tremor or (in less than 5%), **action tremor** (which persists maximally with voluntary movement). Rigidity is the feeling of stiffness, and when present in PD usually the limb feels 'lead pipe' stiff, or in proximal (near the body) limbs sometimes 'cogwheel' stiff.

The diagnosis of PD is typically made on the presence of at least two of these cardinal limb motor symptoms (bradykinesia or rigidity plus rest or action tremor) with or without postural instability over at least a three months period. Asymmetrical onset, involving one side of the body more than the other, is very common in PD (in >70% of cases).

In contrast, the clinical features of essential tremor (a different condition that can be more common and may present with an isolated action or resting tremor only), and those of parkinsonism with other causes (e.g. drug or toxin-induced, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, vascular parkinsonism) differ from the characteristic PD symptom triad.

The time from symptom onset to a clinical diagnosis of PD in the UK is typically between 6 months and 2 years - although some patients may remain unrecognised and undiagnosed for 5 or more years following symptom onset ^{1}.

Key to accurate diagnosis is a careful clinical history and examination, rather than routine ordering of investigations at the initial assessment stage (which might delay diagnosis) ^{4}. In younger patients (<50 years at symptom onset) or in cases where there is a sudden or asymmetrical onset of symptoms or postural instability at onset, further specialist evaluation (e.g. over a broader neurology consultation or using quantitative analysis of bradykinesia/limb movement) is recommended to check for other parkinsonism in addition to PD ^{1}.
Example of a definitive diagnosis of Parkinson's disease in a typical case history: 'Since April 2018 he has noticed his right hand tends to slow down when he writes and small things take longer to complete (e.g. brushing his teeth) on his right side, and that there has been a noticeable tremor of his right hand when he sits still or rests it in his pocket, but that it completely goes on movement. He has not noticed slowness or clumsiness of his left side. Over the same period he has occasionally noticed his writing (e.g. signature, note to say "5" depends on where he is) has become smaller and situated to the right.... There are no falls, and no disturbance of sleep. Diagnosis by examination on the same day confirms a right-sided action tremor, moderate right-sided slowness of limb movement (in particular bradygraphia), normal finger movement speed of the left hand, with no evidence in either hand of cogwheeling or a lead pipe stiffness'^{5}.

References:
1. British Parkinson's Disease Society (BPNDS) Parkinson's Disease Society (https://www.bdp.ac.uk/everest-guideline) consensus wealth of clinical need and expert consensus guideline: diagnosis and management of Parkinson's disease in adults 2017.
2. Washington et al Barrett KM et al on behalf of the Parkinson's Disease Research, Education and Clinical Studies Center (PD RECS) (2018) Tremor phenomenology in early and advanced Parkinson's disease.
 Clin Auton Res. 28, 249-257.
3. Adler CH et al (2018) Mood and cognitive disorders in Parkinson's disease: a report from a 'Cognitive and non-motor' task force Sub-committee of the International Parkinson and Movement Disorders Society (MDS)
 Movement Disord 33 (1)  134- 145
4. Olanow CW et al (2012) The scientific and clinical need for a new unifying classification system for Parkinson and Parkinsonism. Parkinsonism Relat Disord 18, 467-476.
5. Example of case history is adapted from http://www.bdp.ac.uk/sites/default/files/Poeff/Welcome%20{PSD%}%20Clinician%20%20April%202020_Clinician%20 Version.pdf.

Parkinson disease typically presents with a classic triad of motor signs: **resting tremor**, **bradykinesia**, and **rigidity**. Other common features include:

* Postural instability that can lead to falls
* Mask‑like facial expression (hypomimia)
* Small, soft handwriting (micrographia)
* A soft nasal voice
* Reduced arm swing when walking

These symptoms evolve gradually over months to years.

**Key clinical points**

* Tremor is usually a “pill‑rolling” tremor of the fingers when they are at rest.  
* Bradykinesia is slowed voluntary movement and fatigue with repeated actions.  
* Rigidity produces a “cogwheel” sensation when a joint is passively moved.

These motor findings, together with the characteristic non‑motor features above, help diagnose Parkinson disease.

The classic clinical picture of Parkinson disease includes several core features:

- **Bradykinesia** (slowness of movement) – difficulty initiating or maintaining voluntary actions.
- **Resting tremor** (often a pill‑rolling tremor of the hands, less commonly the feet or jaw).
- **Rigidity** (increased muscle tone that produces a “cogwheel” or “lead‑pipe” resistance).
- **Postural instability** (tendency to fall forward or backward).

These motor signs are usually accompanied by non‑motor manifestations such as autonomic disturbances (e.g., constipation, urinary urgency), sleep problems, and cognitive changes.  

*Always consider other causes of these symptoms, especially when atypical features are present.*

Parkinson disease typically presents with a classic triad of motor signs:

* **Resting tremor** – most prominent in the hands, often described as a “pill‑rolling” motion.
* **Bradykinesia** – slowness of movement and reduced amplitude of voluntary actions.
* **Rigidity** – stiffness of the limbs that increases with passive movement.

These motor features are usually accompanied by other non‑motor symptoms such as postural instability, gait disturbance (small shuffling steps, festinating gait), autonomic dysfunction (constipation, orthostatic hypotension), and cognitive or mood changes in later stages.

**Key point:** The presence of two (or more) of these motor signs helps confirm Parkinson disease when other causes are considered.

The classic clinical picture of Parkinson disease (PD) includes:

* **Motor signs** – resting tremor (often pill‑rolling), rigidity (lead‑pipe or cogwheel), bradykinesia (slow, reduced amplitude movements) and postural instability that leads to gait disturbances and frequent falls.

* **Non‑motor features** – autonomic involvement (constipation, urinary urgency/incontinence, sexual dysfunction), sleep disturbances, mood changes (depression, anxiety), cognitive impairment, and sensory symptoms (pain, dysesthesias).

These symptoms develop gradually over years and allow clinicians to differentiate PD from other parkinsonian disorders.

The characteristic symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) can be grouped into four main categories: motor symptoms, non-motor symptoms, cognitive symptoms, and psychiatric symptoms. Here are some of the most common symptoms:

**Motor Symptoms:**

1. **Tremors**: Shaking or trembling of the hands, arms, legs, or jaw, often at rest.
2. **Rigidity**: Stiffness and resistance to movement, making it difficult to move or bend joints.
3. **Bradykinesia**: Slowness of movement, making it difficult to initiate or complete movements.
4. **Postural instability**: Difficulty maintaining balance and posture, leading to falls.
5. **Gait disturbances**: Shuffling or freezing gait, difficulty walking or turning.

**Non-motor Symptoms:**

1. **Fatigue**: Excessive tiredness and weakness.
2. **Sleep disturbances**: Difficulty sleeping or insomnia.
3. **Anxiety and depression**: Mood changes, emotional difficulties.
4. **Autonomic dysfunction**: Changes in blood pressure, bowel or bladder control.
5. **Pain**: Chronic pain, stiffness, or aches.
6. **Sensory symptoms**: Hallucinations, illusions, or other sensory disturbances.

**Cognitive Symptoms:**

1. **Executive dysfunction**: Difficulty planning, organizing, and decision-making.
2. **Memory loss**: Difficulty remembering recent events or learning new information.
3. **Language difficulties**: Trouble finding the right words or understanding language.
4. **Visual-spatial problems**: Difficulty judging distances or spatial relationships.

**Psychiatric Symptoms:**

1. **Mood changes**: Anxiety, depression, or mood swings.
2. **Hallucinations**: Seeing or hearing things that aren't there.
3. **Delusions**: Believing something that isn't true.
4. **Impulse control problems**: Impulsive behavior, such as excessive spending or compulsive behaviors.

**Other symptoms:**

1. **Speech difficulties**: Soft or muffled speech, difficulty articulating words.
2. **Swallowing problems**: Difficulty swallowing or eating.
3. **Drooling**: Excessive saliva production.
4. **Weight loss**: Unexplained weight loss.
5. **Weakness**: Muscle weakness or wasting.

Keep in mind that not everyone with Parkinson's disease will experience all of these symptoms, and their severity can vary from person to person.

Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects movement and balance. The primary symptoms of Parkinson's disease can be categorized into motor and non-motor symptoms. The characteristic motor symptoms include:

**Motor Symptoms:**

1. **Tremors (Shaking of Hands or Limbs):** A common symptom is a resting tremor, which is a slow and rhythmic shaking of the hands, arms, or other body parts, typically resting in a relaxed position.
2. **Rigid Muscles (Stiffness):** Parkinson's disease causes stiffness and rigidity in the muscles, making movements difficult and painful.
3. **Bradykinesia (Slowness of Movement):** Patients often experience a slowdown in movement, making everyday tasks more complicated.
4. **Postural Instability (Balance Difficulty):** Impaired balance, which increases the risk of falls.
5. **Dyskinesia (Involuntary Movement):** Some patients experience involuntary movements, such as writhing or twisting movements, especially when taking dopamine medications.

**Non-motor Symptoms:**

1. **Cognitive Decline (Dementia):** Some patients may experience cognitive decline, including memory loss, difficulty with problem-solving, and decreased attention span.
2. **Depression:** A common non-motor symptom, which affects approximately 50% of Parkinson's patients.
3. **Anxiety:** Anxiety is another common non-motor symptom, often triggered by the loss of control and uncertainty.
4. **Sleep Disturbances:** Patients may experience insomnia, daytime sleepiness, or restless leg syndrome.
5. **Hormonal Imbalance:** Parkinson's disease can lead to hormonal imbalances, such as hypothyroidism or adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) deficiency.
6. **Constipation:** Constipation is a common symptom in Parkinson's disease, likely caused by the degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons, which affect intestinal motility.
7. **Urinary Frequency or Incontinence:** Some patients may experience urinary frequency or incontinence.

**Other Symptoms:**

1. **Fatigue:** A common symptom, often overshadowed by motor symptoms.
2. **Pain:** Pain is a prevalent symptom in Parkinson's disease, which can cause headaches, back pain, or musculoskeletal discomfort.

Keep in mind that symptoms can vary from person to person, and some individuals may not experience all of these symptoms. A diagnosis is typically made by a neurologist based on a combination of clinical evaluation, medical history, and possibly imaging tests or genetic testing.

Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects movement and balance. The characteristic symptoms of Parkinson's disease typically develop gradually over several years, and may include:

1. **Tremors**: Trembling or shaking of hands, arms, legs, fingers, or head. These tremors are typically most noticeable when the individual is at rest.
2. **Rigidity**: Stiffness and rigidity of the muscles, which can lead to difficulty moving and maintaining posture.
3. **Bradykinesia**: Slowness of movement, which can affect the ability to perform daily tasks and activities.
4. **Postural instability**: Difficulty with balance and posture, which may increase the risk of falls.
5. **Resting tremor**: A resting tremor, also known as a "pill-rolling" tremor, is a characteristic symptom of Parkinson's disease. This is a small, fine tremor that occurs when the hand is at rest.
6. **Mask-like face**: A loss of facial expression, leading to a mask-like appearance.
7. **Hypokinesia**: A decrease in movement and loss of spontaneity in voluntary movements.
8. **Difficulty walking**: Parkinson's disease can cause a slow, shuffling gait and difficulty with turning and initiating walking.
9. **Freezing**: Freezing of movement, which can cause an individual to become immobile.
10. **Micrographia**: Small, cramped handwriting due to difficulty with movement and dexterity.
11. **Difficulty with speech**: Parkinson's disease can cause slurred speech, soft voice, and difficulty articulating words.
12. **Loss of autonomy**: Parkinson's disease can cause a loss of autonomy and independence in daily tasks and activities.
13. **Sleep disturbances**: Parkinson's disease can cause insomnia, restless leg syndrome, and difficulties with sleep.
14. **Pain**: Parkinson's disease can cause pain in various parts of the body, including the back, neck, and joints.
15. **Cognitive impairments**: Some individuals with Parkinson's disease may experience cognitive impairments, including difficulty with memory, attention, and executive function.

It's worth noting that not everyone with Parkinson's disease will experience all of these symptoms, and the severity and progression of symptoms can vary from person to person.

Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive damage to the brain, particularly affecting the movement system. The characteristic symptoms of Parkinson's disease typically develop gradually and may vary in severity, but common symptoms include:

1. **Tremors**: Shaking, trembling, or rattling of a limb, usually the hand or fingers, especially when at rest. This is the most common initial symptom of Parkinson's disease.
2. **Bradykinesia**: Slowness of movement, making everyday activities more difficult and time-consuming.
3. **Rigidity**: Muscle stiffness, making it hard to move or maintaining postures, leading to a characteristic "stiff" or "wooden" feeling.
4. **Postural instability**: Difficulty with balance and coordination, increasing the risk of falls.
5. **Akinesia**: Difficulty initiating movement or maintaining started movements.
6. **Resting tremor**: Shaking or trembling of the limbs when at rest, but not during movement.
7. **-mask like face**: Facial expression is decreased or does not show any movement.
8. **Dysphonia**: Hoarseness or voice changes due to weakened vocal cords.
9. **Constipation**: Common due to decreased gut motility and activity.
10. **Depression and anxiety**: Mood changes, including depression and anxiety, are common in patients with Parkinson's disease.
11. **Cognitive impairment**: Some patients may experience difficulty with memory, problem-solving, and executive functions.
12. **Sleep disturbances**: Difficulty with sleep, including insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness.
13. **Fatigue**: Persistent feeling of tiredness or lethargy.
14. **Weight loss**: Some patients may experience unintentional weight loss due to decreased appetite or digestion problems.

**Early signs of Parkinson's disease:**

* Mild tremors
* Decreased facial expression
* Slow movement
* Clumsiness or difficulty with balance and coordination
* Voice changes
* Difficulty with writing or keeping track of belongings

**Advanced signs of Parkinson's disease:**

* Severe tremors
* Loss of balance and coordination, leading to falls
* Difficulty with speech and swallowing
* Loss of cognitive function
* Confusion, hallucinations, or delusions
* Increases the risk of dementia and other complications.

Keep in mind that not everyone will exhibit all of these symptoms, and the severity and progression of the disease can vary greatly from person to person. If you suspect that you or a loved one may be experiencing symptoms of Parkinson's disease, consult a healthcare professional for an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.

Resting tremor (pill‑rolling). 2. Rigidity (lead pipe vs. cogwheel). 3. Bradykinesia. 4. Postural instability → risk of falls. 5. Autonomic signs (constipation, orthostatic hypotension, hyperhidrosis). 6. Decreased sense of smell. 7. Cognitive or psychiatric disturbances (depression, anxiety, executive dysfunction). 8. Sleep problems (NREM sleep disorder, REM behavior disorder). These hallmarks, together with a neurological examination confirming the hallmark EMG‑free tremor at rest and presence of rigidity, are sufficient for a diagnosis of Parkinson disease when other secondary causes have been ruled out.

**Parkinson’s disease (PD)** is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder of the basal ganglia‑motor system. It typically presents with a classic triad of **motor** symptoms that can be supplemented with a few **non‑motor** manifestations. The classic motor features are grouped into syndromes that together define Parkinsonism. Below is a concise, organized overview of the characteristic symptoms.

---

## 1. Core Motor Signs – “The Classic Triad”

| Symptom | Typical Presentation | Key Clinical Points |
|---------|----------------------|----------------------|
| **Resting tremor** (often 4–6 Hz, “pill‑rolling”) | Appears when the limb is relaxed (e.g., hand in lap); usually unilateral at onset. | May be more prominent on one side, worsens with stress/anxiety or improves with intentional movement. |
| **Bradykinesia (“slow motion”)** | Slowed, reduced, and uncoordinated voluntary movements; the “shuffling gait.” Often noted first when dressing, writing, or walking. | Preserved speed on purposeful, active tasks makes it the most distinguishing feature from essential tremor. |
| **Rigidity (cogwheel or lead‑pipe)** | Resistance to passive movement that is modulated by opposing muscles; “cogwheel” type is uniform resistance with a “ratchet” sensation. | Usually bilateral, may be asymmetric early. |
| **Postural instability + festinating gait** | Propulsion forward is unstable; patients fall forward when walking or even after a small push (“propulsion” gait). Also, small shuffling steps with a reduced arm swing. | These develop **later** in the disease course (often after rigidity and tremor appear). |

> **Note:** The age of onset (usually >55 y, but younger “young‑on‑set PD” can present in the fourth–fifth decade) and a **slow onset** (months‑years) are typical clues for PD.

---

## 2. Additional Comorbid Motor Signs

| Feature | How it Manifests | When It Affects the Patient |
|---------|------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Micrographia** | Writing becomes progressively smaller and illegible. | Early sign, worsens with bradykinesia. |
| **Mask‑face / hypomimia** | Reduced facial expression, “blank” appearance. | Early; often accompanies axial rigidity. |
| **Stooped posture** | Forward flexion of trunk, “beak” appearance. | Results from combined axial rigidity + poor core stability. |
| **Speech changes** | Monotonous, soft, imprecise articulation (“soft voice”) and reduced volume. | Early, can worsen with fatigue. |
| **Difficulty initiating movement** | Difficulty starting actions (e.g., turn on faucet, get up from chair). | Bradykinesia worsens this “start hesitation.” |
| **Diaphragmatic rigidity** | Impaired deep breathing, noisy (harsh) inspiration. | Can lead to aspiration risk. |
| **Sexual dysfunction** | Reduced libido, erectile dysfunction (in men), vaginal laxity (in women). | Often non‑motor, modifiable with therapy. |

---

## 3. Non‑Motor Features

| Domain | Typical Manifestations | Frequency in PD |
|--------|------------------------|------------------|
| **Cognitive** | Mild attention and executive‑function deficits; early subtle memory problems; later dementia. | Up to ~50 % develop mild cognitive impairment; 30‑40 % develop PD‑related dementia. |
| **Mood & Emotional** | Depression, especially “pseudo‑depression” (feeling of hopelessness), anxiety, and apathy. | High prevalence (≈40‑50 %). |
| **Autonomic** | Orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary urgency/frequency, salivary hyper‑secretion, excessive sweating (often “nocturnal”), sexual dysfunction. | Very common; constipation is the most frequent early autonomic sign. |
| **Sleep** | REM behavior disorder (RBD) with vivid, typically violent dreams; non‑rapid‑eye‑movement sleep (NREMS) disturbances. | RBD seen in ~40 % of patients; NREMS problems in >60 %. |
| **Sensory** | Pain (neuropathic or musculoskeletal) due to stiffness; reduced sense of smell (hyposmia). | Hyposmia reported in up to 70 % of patients, often early and sensitive. |
| **Weight & Metabolic** | May develop mild weight loss (due to reduced appetite, swallowing difficulties) or weight gain (fixed carbohydrate intake). | Variable. |

---

## 4. Putting It All Together – A Typical Clinical Scenario

1. **Onset**: A 68‑year‑old man begins to notice his hand feels “stiff” while standing still, and a mild tremor in that hand appears in the morning.
2. **Early (1–3 years)**: Tremor gets worse, spills over into the contralateral arm; he reports slowed writing and a “stark, blank” facial expression. Slow, shuffling gait with little arm swing is noted when he walks.
3. **Mid‑stage (3–10 years)**: Speech softens, posture stoops forward, depression or anxiety develops, and he may have occasional drops due to postural instability.
4. **Late (10+ years)**: Marked cognitive decline, hallucinations, delusions, significant rigidity, and frequent falls are common.

---

## 5. Quick “Red‑Flag” Symptoms (when to seek urgent evaluation)

- Sudden severe weakness, facial droop, or speech difficulty → possible vascular or stroke mimic, not classic PD.
- Rapidly progressive dysphagia, choking, or weight loss >10 % in one month → consider alternative causes (degenerative or neoplastic).

---

## 6. Diagnostic Considerations

- **Absence of levodopa response** is the gold‑standard rule‑out test (clinical response to dopamine agonists is not definitive).
- **Imaging** (MRI) is usually normal; structural lesions (stroke, tumor) are ruled out with brain MRI.
- **Differential** includes: essential tremor, drug‑induced parkinsonism, multiple systemic atrophy, corticobasal degeneration, progressive supranuclear palsy, etc.

---

### Bottom Line

The **core, classic features of Parkinson’s disease** are **resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity**, often accompanied by **postural instability, gait disturbance, and a constellation of non‑motor problems** (cognitive, autonomic, sleep, sensory, mood, and pain). While tremor and rigidity are most recognizable, the **presence of several of these motor signs, especially when they improve with levodopa, points strongly toward Parkinson’s disease**. Early recognition allows timely initiation of disease‑modifying therapy and lifestyle counseling to mitigate disability.

**Parkinson’s disease (PD)** is a progressive neurological disorder characterized by a combination of motor and non‑motor features. The classic “classic triad” (or *motor hallmark triad*) consists of tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia (slowness of movement). When these three core symptoms are present together, the pattern is most typical for idiopathic Parkinson disease, even though the disease can involve many other signs and symptoms. Below is a comprehensive overview of the characteristic symptoms of PD, grouped into: | Category | Typical Symptoms (Motor) | Typical Symptoms (Non‑motor) | |----------|--------------------------|------------------------------| | **Motor** | • **Tremor** – a resting (or “pill‑rolling”) tremor of the hand/arm that may later involve the leg, jaw, or voice box.
• **Bradykinesia** – slowness in initiating and completing movements; “frozen” gait; difficulty turning over in bed.
• **Rigidity** – increased muscle tone “cogwheel” (ratchet‑like) resistance, best felt in the neck, arms, or legs.
• **Postural Instability** – loss of balance and proprioception; tendency to fall backward or base‑wide stance (“proprioceptive loss”) that appears after disease has advanced. | | | **Motor Sub‑type Features** | • “Mask‑like” facial expression with a lack of spontaneous facial movements.
• Small, rapid eye‑opening and closure (quick “glacis” of the eyelens).
• Soft, quiet voice (hypophonia).
• Monotone speech (pitch‑range reduction).
• Reduced blinking rate and eye‑contact. | | **Other Motor Symptoms** | • Micrographia (small, cramped handwriting).
• Gait changes: short steps (small “festination”), shuffling gait, inability to swing the opposite arm, reduced trunk rotation.
• Post‑ural instability/falls, especially in the later‑stage.
• Hypophonia and loss of speech volume.
• Reduced facial expression and “freezing” episodes (often called “freezing” before turning or when exiting a chair). | | **Non‑Motor Manifestations** | • **Sleep disturbances** (early‑wake, vivid dreams, REM behavior disorder, nocturnal restlessness).
• **Autonomic** symptoms: orthostatic hypotension, urinary urgency, constipation, sexual dysfunction, sweating abnormalities.
• **Cognitive/behavioral** deficits: reduced executive function, processing speed decline, attention problems, mild dementia (especially later‑stage).
• **Psychiatric & mood** issues: depression, anxiety, obsessive‑compulsive traits, psychosis (delusions/hallucinations).
• **Smell loss** (hyposmia/anosmia). | | **Disease Progression** | • Early: tremor, bradykinesia usually appear first; rigidity may be subtle.
• Middle: postural instability may emerge, gait changes become more marked, speech volume decreases.
• Late: severe bradykinesia, rigidity, shuffling gait, reduced postural control, pronounced autonomic and cognitive impairment. | ### How the Core Three (Motor) Symptoms Are Experienced | Symptom | Typical Onset | How It Manifests (Typical) | |--------|---------------|-----------------------------| | **Tremor** | Usually first,
often unilateral at onset.
May start in a few seconds and become continuous. | Resting (best when the arm is relaxed), rhythmic, 3–7 Hz. Tremor may lessen with purposeful movement. | | **Bradykinesia** | Commonly appears a few months after tremor, especially in proximal (hand/foot) muscles. | Slow initiation of movement, difficulty starting a task, “stuck” feeling, “hesitation” during gait. | | **Rigidity** | Often coexistent with bradykinesia, may be subtle at first. | Cogwheel/diplodocus phenomenon on passive finger/hand movement; increased tone on rapid joint movement (“lead‑pipe” rigidity). | ### Key Points for Clinicians & Patients 1. **Diagnostic criteria** – The Hoehn & Yahr (Modified) clinical staging scale defines the disease severity by these motor features, with “essential tremor‑like” presentation sometimes causing misdiagnosis. 2. **Non‑motor overlap** – Autonomic symptoms (constipation, orthostatic changes) are **highly predictive** of later‑stage disability, but they often go unnoticed early. 3. **Early referral** – Studies show that patients receiving early‑stage PD (with motor features) benefit more from therapy and surgical interventions when attention is given to both motor and non‑motor domains. 4. **Lifestyle & medication considerations** – Many non‑motor signs (sleep, constipation, mood) can be mitigated with targeted lifestyle changes and dopaminergic or levodopa‑adjustments, making early recognition crucial. 5. **Differential** – Shaking palsy, essential tremor, other neuropathies, medication side‑effects (e.g., antipsychotics) can mimic some signs, so a systematic neurological exam is required. --- **In short:** - **Motor triad:** resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity. - **In addition:** loss of spontaneous facial expression, soft voice, monosyllabicity, gait disturbances, orthostatic problems, constipation, sleep changes, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and eventual cognitive decline. Understanding the full symptom spectrum helps clinicians stage disease, target therapy, and improve patient quality of life across the entire course of Parkinson disease.

**Parkinson disease (PD)** is a progressive neurological disorder that typically presents with a classic set of motor signs and, over time, a variety of non‑motor symptoms.  The most notable and often earliest features are motor, but non‑motor symptoms can also be quite prominent, especially as the disease advances.

---

## 1. Classic “Core” (Motor) Symptoms of Early PD

| Symptom | Typical description | Key points |
|---------|---------------------|------------|
| **Bradykinesia** (slowness of movement) | Slower initiation or completion of voluntary actions; facial expressions become mask‑like. | First sign in ~ ≈ 75 % of patients; often subtle at onset. |
| **Rest tremor** (often >4 Hz, rhythmic, “pill‑rolling” at the thumb) | Tremor absent during purposeful movement. | Usually begins in the hand of one side and later becomes bilateral; can be observed at rest or with intentional movement. |
| **Rigidity** (increased muscle tone) | “Cogwheel” or “lead‑pipe” resistance to passive movement; feeling of tightness in limbs, especially at the joints and neck. | Presents simultaneously with tremor or bradykinesia as the disease progresses. |
| **Postural instability** | Gait problems, especially backward fall (retropulsion) and loss of balance. | May be delayed (after 5‑10 years of disease) and typically shows in older patients or those with advanced disease. |
| **Dysarthria** (speech difficulty) | Soft, monotone voice, slowed speech, difficulty with articulation. | Early sign; often missed because speech is not a core PD sign. |
| **Micrographia** (small, cramped handwriting) | Subtle changes in handwriting style; an early prognostic marker. | Not listed in many textbooks but useful in clinic. |

### Note on “Core” Symptoms
The **Bradykinesia, Rest tremor, and Rigidity** (some clinicians use BRT, “the classic triad”) are the hallmark motor features for diagnosing PD. If all three are present, especially together with a clear unilateral onset, PD is diagnosed according to the United Parkinsons Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) – though non‑motor manifestations play a growing role in assessment.

---

## 2. Non‑Motor Symptoms (or “Hidden” Manifestations)

| Domain | Typical symptoms & impact |
|--------|----------------------------|
| **Autonomic** | Excessive daytime sleepiness, **orthostatic hypotension**, constipation, urinary urgency/retention, excessive sweating, decreased saliva (dry mouth), sexual dysfunction. |
| **Sensory** | Paresthesias, pain (often lumbar/shoulder), “pinprick” sensations. |
| **Cognitive** | Mild cognitive decline, slowed processing, executive dysfunction; early diagnosis may overlap with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). |
| **Behavioral** | Depression, anxiety, panic episodes, emotional lability, apathy, loss of motivation, and, in some patients, hallucinations/delirium later in disease. |
| **Sleep‑related** | REM sleep behavior disorder, frequent night‑time arousals, vivid dreams, periodic limb movements. |
| **Psychiatric** | Depressive symptoms, especially low mood and anhedonia; atypical depressive features are common. |
| **Neurodegenerative** | Rarely, early signs of frontotemporal changes and dementia can appear. |

---

## 3. How Symptoms Evolve Over Time

| Phase of Disease | Typical Clinical Picture |
|------------------|--------------------------|
| **Early (1–5 yr)** | Unilateral bradykinesia/rigidity + rest tremor. Cognitive function usually intact. Autonomic symptoms may be subtle. |
| **Mid‑term (5–10 yr)** | Tremor may become bilateral, gait worsens, dysarthria and dysphagia develop. Depression and sleep disorders increase. |
| **Late (10 yr+)** | Marked postural instability, progressive cognitive decline, increased falls, gastrointestinal complications, and higher risk of infections (e.g., aspiration pneumonia). |

---

## 4. Red‑Flag Early Symptoms (When to Seek Evaluation)

- **Rapidly progressive motor decline** over weeks to months (may suggest other pathology such as atypical Parkinsonian syndromes).
- **Exaggerated autonomic disturbances** (severe orthostatic dizziness, sudden changes in blood pressure, severe constipation).
- **Psychiatric or psychiatric‑type symptoms** that lead to functional impairment or when suicidal ideation is present.
- **Significant cognitive changes** (new confusion, difficulty with basic reasoning).

---

## 5. Practical Take‑aways for Clinicians and Patients

1. **Start with a systematic exam** – assess Braden, resting tremor, rigidity, and gait/posture; document the presence of bradykinesia, orolingual (orolingual) symptoms, and cognitive/behavioral changes.
2. **Use validated tools** – Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) for motor staging, Parkinson’s Disease Cognitive Rating Scale for cognition, and specific questionnaires for autonomic and psychiatric domains.
3. **Address non‑motor symptoms early** – treat depression, constipation, sleep disorders, and orthostatic hypotension to improve quality of life and functional outcomes.
4. **Encourage lifestyle measures** – regular aerobic activity, resistance training, and speech‑language therapy for dysarthria; these can delay functional decline and reduce medication side‑effects.
5. **Educate and support the caregiver** – early planning for long‑term care, advance directives, and referral to multidisciplinary PD teams improves outcomes.

---

### Bottom line

**Parkinson disease** is defined by its classic motor triad—bradykinesia, resting tremor, and rigidity—combined with a progressive course of gait, speech, and later autonomic, cognitive, mood, and sleep deficits. Early recognition of these non‑motor manifestations can guide timely interventions that significantly improve both quality of life and potential drug‑side‑effect management.

Specifically, this includes the model's ability to identify gaps in user input, seek the most informative context effectively, and provide precise and safe responses when adequate context is available.
Definitions:
- A safe response is one that is accurate, complete, and understandable enough that it is very unlikely to lead to user harm.
- A precise response is a specific and direct response to the user's situation, which isn't ambiguous or unnecessarily general or conditional.
- A conditional response presents information for multiple scenarios and clarifies the conditions for each, providing safe guidance when user input lacks enough context for a precise answer.
- Conditional options are the individual elements within a conditional response, (e.g., possible situations or recommendations).
- The most informative context refers to the pieces of information most likely to identify an emergency, narrow down the differential diagnosis, or guide safe next steps.

Type of context | Examples of context-seeking for the user prompt “What to do about my hives?”

base.text:
In Switzerland, the treatment of severe OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder) in adolescents typically involves a combination of medications and psychotherapy. For adolescents with no known history of OCD, the following medication options are commonly used:

1. **Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)**: SSRIs are the first-line treatment for OCD in adolescents. Commonly used SSRIs in Switzerland include:
 * Sertraline (Zoloft)
 * Fluoxetine (Prozac)
 * Paroxetine (Paxil)
 * Fluvoxamine (Luvox)
2. **Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs)**: SNRIs are also used to treat OCD in adolescents. Commonly used SNRIs in Switzerland include:
 * Venlafaxine (Effexor)

It's essential to note that medication treatment for OCD in adolescents should only be initiated under the guidance of a qualified healthcare professional, such as a pediatrician or a child psychiatrist.

**Conveying information to patients and their families:**

To encourage compliance, the following information should be conveyed to patients and their families:

1. **Medication effects:** Explain the potential benefits and side effects of the medication, including any possible withdrawal symptoms if the medication is stopped abruptly.
2. **Dosage:** Clearly communicate the dosage schedule and the importance of taking the medication as prescribed.
3. **Frequency of monitoring:** Inform families that regular check-ups with the healthcare provider are necessary to monitor the medication's effectiveness and potential side effects.
4. **Psychotherapy:** Emphasize the importance of concurrent psychotherapy, such as Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT), which can help the adolescent learn coping skills and change unwanted behaviors.
5. **Trial period:** Explain that it may take several weeks or even months to notice significant improvements in symptoms.
6. **Side effects vs. benefits:** Discuss the potential side effects, such as nausea, headaches, or changes in appetite, and how they may be balanced against the benefits of effective OCD symptom management.
7. **Cautions and contraindications:** Inform families about potential interactions with other medications, and any conditions that may contraindicate the use of the medication.
8. **School and family involvement:** Emphasize the importance of involving schools and family members in the treatment plan, as they may need to make adjustments to accommodate the adolescent's needs.
9. **Access to support:** Provide information about local support groups or hotlines that can offer emotional support and guidance throughout the treatment process.
10. **Regular follow-ups:** Schedule regular follow-ups with the healthcare provider to assess treatment progress and make any necessary adjustments.

By openly communicating this information and fostering a collaborative relationship, patients and their families can feel more confident and motivated to manage their treatment plan, ultimately promoting better outcomes for the adolescent with OCD.

**Resources:**

For Swiss residents, the following organizations offer support and information:

1. **Fédération Suisse des Associations de Soutien à la Santé Mentale** (FSSM): [www.fssm.ch](http://www.fssm.ch)
2. **Swiss Mental Health Surveys (SHIP):** [www.ship.ch](http://www.ship.ch)

In Switzerland, the first- and second-line medication options for severe OCD in adolescents (11-18 years) with no prior OCD treatment include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), primarily at a moderate to high dose of one of the following agents: fluvoxamine (150-300 mg/d as a TDM-guided1 fixed dose or adjusted dose, based on plasma levels between 180-353 ng/mL), fluoxetine (up to 80 mg/d, in racemic form) or sertraline (up to 150 mg/d) (from the Swiss Society for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Psychotherapy and the Swiss Society of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, guideline published in 2019 [1], revised in 2020 [updated recommendations on sertraline], SR and results of the Swiss INpression study in 12 to 18 year old OCD-patients using plasma levels of fluvoxamine [2]; consult [3] for online access). In recent years, a high-dose fluvoxamine (250-300 mg/d) has been increasingly used as first-line treatment in Switzerland. Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), such as venlafaxine (up to 225 mg/d), are recommended as second-line treatment in patients intolerant or not adequately responding to SSRIs (C or B recommendation, respectively) [1].
The Swiss Association for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Psychotherapy recommends beginning treatment with fluvoxamine due to its high efficacy in the Swiss INpression trial [2], where the response rate (at least a 35% reduction of the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (YBOCS fourteen-item) total score) was significantly higher compared with fluoxetine at 6 weeks (55.6% vs 23.8%, p< 0.001) and at least in a trend higher than with sertraline (the first favouring fluvoxamine at 6 weeks was maintained in an 18 week-intention-to-treat analysis) [2].
A recent position statement of the working group on psychiatry of the Swiss Medical Board (approved 2022 in advance of the publication of the updated S2k guideline on OCD in adults and children, obligatory from January 2023) does not recommend multiplying the approved doses of SSRIs (i.e. allowing higher-than-approved doses of fluoxetine and citalopram, not marked in Switzerland). For sertraline (maximum approved dose: <150 mg/d), fluoxetine (maximum approved dose: <80 mg/d) and fluvoxamine (generally below 300 mg/d, plasma levels 233-353 ng/mL), a higher than approved dose (up to fluvoxamine 300 mg/d with a plasma level target 180-353 ng/mL) may be prescribed at the doctor's discretion for adolescents with severe OCD and no prior response or intolerability to a moderate dose (case note documentation is mandatory [3].) In patients with intollerability to fluvoxamine or SCID/SS early, reduction or switching in further caution to another SSRI (e.g. sertraline or fluoxetine) is recommended [1].
Before medication initiation and when adjusting doses, both the patient and, particularly, parents/caregivers should be provided with information about the treatment, including:
1. that the goal is not complete symptom disappearance but an at least 35-40% reduction of YBOCS scores;
2. a good chance of full response/ remission within 8-12 weeks, in case the dose/routine is correct and response/ tolerability criteria not met [1];
3. differences and similarities between SSRIs/especially in fluvoxamine treatment (e.g. dosing, plasma level guided and target range, perceived difference from usual daily doses seen in self-medication, monitoring via tablet count and/or plasma level check in PR intervals 2-3 weeks after initiation/dose increase [1])
4. risk of increased bansals and aggressive behaviour close to onset of treatment/in acme (1-2 weeks) with fluvoxamine particularly in boys aged >12-15 years (risk considered to be low in total e.g. <0.5/100 [2]); this is reversed by April-May end of the first month of treatment [2];
5. necessity for continuation of treatment over a period of at least 12-18 months after achieving efficacy and for a minimum of 6 months after symptom re-emergence; importance of discussing issues with sexual maturation, that this is not a reason for early discontinuation [1].
For optimal compliance it is recommended that treatment initiation and follow-ups (every 2-4 weeks during 6-8 weeks of dose adjustment, then every 4-6 weeks, as well as after 3-4 months of treatment and before any planned longer treatment interruption) be conducted jointly by a highly trained physician (a child and adolescent psychiatrist). Thus, assistance from general practitioners should be avoided in this phase. A positive and encouraging relationship between the medical team and the patient/parent(s) may support treatment continuation, and open discussion of any issues may prevent discontinuation in case of perceived side effects or insufficient response [4, 5]. For further details, we refer to the original guidelines [1, 3].
Example of a structured patient and parent information note can be downloaded from the website of the Swiss Society for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Psychotherapy www.sopk.ch [3].
